speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PETITION REQUESTING DECLARATION OF ASSINIBOINE VALLEY AS DISASTER AREA
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that the Clerk has laid on the table the 20th report of the clerk of petitions. In that report the clerk of petitions says that the petition of the following- which is the one of J. L. C. Carter of Peters-field, Manitoba, and others presented on April 11 by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce)-meets the requirements of standing order 70 as to form. However, the clerk in connection with this petition has given me an opinion which reads as follows:
It is my duty to inform you that although the petition presented Wednesday. April 11, by Mr. Bryce meets the requirements of standing order 70 as to form, it is irregular in so far as it asks the house to consider the granting of financial assistance.
The petitioners pray that this house may be pleased to consider:
(a)	The advisability of declaring the flooded Assiniboine river valley and the interlake area a disaster area;
(b)	The granting of financial assistance on the basis of $5 per productive acre flooded during the 1955 crop year, which would assist us to maintain our farm homes and to put in a crop this coming spring.
It is my submission that, in accordance with section 54 of the British North America Act, 1867, it is not lawful for the house either to receive or to consider a petition or any other measure involving the expenditure of public money unless the expenditure has been first recommended to the house by a message of the governor general. In dealing with the provisions of section 54 of the British North America Act, Bourinot at page 407 of his fourth edition has this to say:
"No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer."
May in his fifteenth edition, page 654, deals with the financial initiative of the crown, in the following words:
"The sovereign, being the executive power, is charged with the management of all the revenue of the state, and with all payments for the public service. The crown, therefore, acting with the advice of its responsible ministers, makes known to the commons the pecuniary necessities of the government; the commons, in return, grant such aids or supplies as are required to satisfy these demands: and they provide by taxes, and by the appropriation of other sources of the public income, the ways and means to meet the supplies which they have granted. Thus the crown demands money, the commons grant it, and the
lords assent to the grant; but the commons do not vote money unless it be required by the crown." ... If this petition were to be received and considered, the house in my opinion would be dealing not only with a direct request for a grant of money out of the public revenues, but it also would be deciding the quantum of the proposed grant.
There is no doubt in my mind that it has been an unbroken practice in our house to reject petitions directly praying for the granting of money out of the public revenues. (See Bourinot's fourth edition, page 237; also Beauchesne's third edition, citations 608 and 621.)
For these reasons, it is my considered opinion that the petition is out of order and therefore it should not be received.
Respectfully submitted,
(Sgd) Leon J. Raymond.
I concur in this opinion, and therefore I rule the petition cannot be received.

speechtext:
Hon. members will notice on today's order paper at page 12 that there are two notices of motions that are still printed notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 15 (4).
On Wednesday, March 21 last, two motions for the production of papers were transferred to "Notices of Motions" by virtue of the latter part of standing order 47:
". . . but if on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the Clerk to the order of 'Notices of Motions' ".
At the time there was one private members' Monday still available out of the six provided by standing order 15 (3).
The last private members' day was spent on March 26.
Standing order 15 (4) states that after the fifth sitting day following the expiry of Monday as a private members' day, notices of motions shall not be printed on the order paper.
Yesterday, Wednesday, April 11, was the fifth sitting day following the expiry of Mondays as private members' days.
It is one of the numerous duties of the Clerk to attend to the preparation of the order paper (see standing order 84).

Standing Order No. 47 On the day immediately following the last private member's Monday, namely, on Tuesday, March 27 last, I wrote to the Clerk as follows:
My dear Mr. Raymond:
I wish to follow up the ruling that I made on March 21 last, regarding the transfer of a motion under standing order 47, a ruling in which you concurred.
At the time of the ruling there was one private members' day left, and it was spent yesterday, Monday, March 26. Because of some of the remarks that were made at the time of the ruling, I expected that yesterday some member would, shortly after the opening of the house, use standing order 24 and move "that the orders of the day be now read". If that motion had carried, the motion could then be moved by virtue of standing order 44 "that the house do proceed to order No. 35 under 'Notices of Motions' ", namely, the motion for production of papers transferred at the request of Mr. Pickersgill under the latter part of standing order 47. However, no one tried to have that notice of motion reached.
Now that the sixth private members' day has expired we must take a look at standing order 15 (4):
"Notwithstanding the listing of 'Notices of Motions' as an item of daily business in section (3) of this order, such notices shall not be printed on the order paper after the fifth sitting day following the expiry of Monday as a private members' day".
It is my considered opinion that when standing order 15 (4) was adopted by the committee last year, the "Notices of Motions" to be affected were those introduced on the order paper after notice under standing order 48. Now that all private members' days have been exhausted, "Notices of Motions" appearing on the order paper by virtue of standing order 48, will not be printed on the order paper in consequence of the provisions of standing order 15 (4) but standing order 15 (4) was never meant to and does not affect "Notices of Motions" transferred under the latter part of standing order 47. In my opinion, motions that have been transferred or motions that will be transferred under the latter part of standing order 47, whether private members' days have expired or not, have to be printed under "Notices of Motions". The purpose of transferring a "notice of motion" under the latter part of standing order 47 is to have a debate. It is obvious that when we amended the rules last year we overlooked the passage of the necessary consequential amendments in order to make good the right of debate in relation to the right of transfer given to any member in the latter part of standing order 47. It is clear to me that once all private members' days have expired, the right to transfer should be upheld by the house only if the right to debate the transferred motion is assured. It will be, of course, the responsibility of the house, and particularly of the leader of the house (Beauchesne's third edition, citations 136, 9 and 10), to provide the opportunity to debate any motion so transferred.
In the circumstances, if you agree, I would advise you to have printed under the listing "notices of motions" all motions which may have been transferred or may be transferred under the latter part of standing order 47.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd) L. Rene Beaudoin, Speaker.

To that letter I received from the Clerk the following reply on March 28:
Dear Mr. Speaker:
In reply to your letter of March 27, it also seems to me that the committee on procedure did not intend to have the provisions of standing order 15 (4) apply to motions for the production of papers which have been transferred to the heading "notices of motions" pursuant to standing order 47. Accordingly, I propose to continue for the duration of the session the daily printing of any motion for the production of papers that has been or which may be transferred to the heading "notices of motions".
I have read carefully your ruling of Wednesday, March 21 last, and the remarks made on the point of order at that time by several members. Although it is not for me to comment upon a Speaker's ruling, I venture to say that, according to practice, you had no alternative to the course which you pursued at that time. In every precedent which I have been able to find, the same course has been followed without exception.
If it is desirable to have a change made in a procedure based on a standing order and supported by an invariable practice, even though that procedure may not have been used very often, the responsibility for taking corrective steps rests, in my opinion, with the house.
It is obviously impracticable to provide for a debate by standing order 47 and, on the other hand, to prohibit debate on the same question by virtue of standing order 15 (3).
To my mind, the transfer of a motion for the production of papers should be conditional in every case upon an assurance that there will be an opportunity to debate the same.
Respectfully submitted,
(Sgd) Leon J. Raymond.
The same reasoning must apply to any question which could be transferred to notices of motions under standing order 39(4), which reads as follows:
(4) If, in the opinion of Mr. Speaker, a question on the order paper put to a minister of the crown is of such a nature as to require a lengthy reply, he may, upon a request made by the government during the question period on Wednesday, direct the same to stand as a notice of motion, and to be transferred to its proper place as such upon the order paper, the clerk of the house being authorized to amend the same as to matters of form.
I wrote again to the Clerk on April 11, 1956, as follows:
Dear Mr. Raymond:
Please refer to my letter of March 27 and your reply of March 28, 1956.
The same procedure should, I believe, be followed if paragraph 4 of standing order 39 were to be taken advantage of.
I could find only one precedent for the use of standing order 39 (4) which appears in Hansard, Vol. 1, February 16, 1923, pages 343 and 344.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) L. Rene Beaudoin, Speaker.
This correspondence speaks for itself and I do hope that this ruling will meet with the approval of the house, which is the master of its own procedure and may use it in any way it pleases to carry out its wishes.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 11, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the theme of what I wish to say today will differ from that of any other speaker in this debate. I do not propose to discuss any of the financial proposals contained in the budget 67509-1814
The Budget-Mr. Simmons but rather I wish to link my remarks to the trade aspects of the finance minister's statement, especially Canada-United States trade. If what I propose to advocate is carried into effect, I am satisfied that an improvement in trade relationships between Canada and the United States will result and that the economy of British Columbia, the Yukon Territory and the territory of Alaska will undoubtedly be substantially strengthened.
Sometimes hon. members in this house, intentionally or otherwise, place a road block across the traffic flow of government business. This results from their efforts to call attention to a certain situation or condition of affairs which, at least to them, constitutes a matter of urgent public importance. Today, sir, I want to draw the attention of the government, the house and the country to a matter which I believe all hon. members will admit truly merits the title of vital public business. What I wish to discuss is certainly vital to the future of Canada's northwest and, I think, to the future of the whole Canadian nation. In raising this matter I am not introducing it as a road block to the business of this house but rather as a stepping stone to progress. If the right kind of action is taken, it will result in the most important single advance in the history of economic development in the northwest and in Alaska.
The community of interests shared by the United States and Canada for more than a century has nourished and stimulated one of the most significant partnerships in the whole long history of international relationships. Not only have the two nations enjoyed long, unbroken political friendship, but their effective co-operation in the economic sphere has been a major factor in winning for North America world leadership in private enterprise achievements and in creating high standards of living for the people of this favoured continent. In the matter of fisheries control, St. Lawrence seaway, Canol pipeline, the Alaska highway, airport bases and radar systems-to mention a few of them-Canada and the United States have tackled thorny international problems and worked together to produce practical solutions that have been an example to the world in co-operation and compromise.
There is yet another complicated situation in which the spirit of give and take and of international teamwork will produce on this continent even more far-reaching benefits and results. A glance at the map will show the Alaska panhandle to be, to all intents and purposes, an economic island, its natural lines of land communication passing through Canadian territory. In the same way, Yukon territory and northern British Columbia are isolated in an economic sense because their
2854	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Simmons natural channels of water communication lead into harbours located along the Alaska panhandle at Skagway, Haines, Juneau, and Wrangell to mention four of them. It is to be hoped that common sense rather than sentiment will soon win out and unravel this complex and wholly unnecessary impasse so that means will be found to advance and expedite the progress and development of the Yukon, northern British Columbia and Alaska. It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I lay this matter before the house at this time for consideration.
There is perhaps no other part of the world where two nations have more closely similar problems, conditions and objectives than have Canada and the United States in their lands, in the northwest of this continent. The development of these extensive areas, so necessary in the broad national interests of both countries, depends primarly on efficient, unobstructed transportation. That primary condition does not exist today. Some early definite move looking toward co-operative action in this direction is urgently indicated.
At the base or root of the transportation problem is the long, narrow strip of coastal territory commonly known as the Alaska panhandle. This strip serves to shut off access to the Pacific coast as far south as 54 degrees north latitude so far as Yukon Territory and roughly one-half of the province of British Columbia are concerned. There is no question that the existence of this land barrier is restricting the economical development of the Canadian northwest and for the same reasons is not helpful to the growth and prosperity of the United States ports along the Alaska panhandle.
I wish to make it clear that Canadians are not the only ones asking for a solution to this restrictive situation. A number of United States mining companies operating at points and in areas adjacent to the panhandle want to be rid of unnecessary boundary complications.
In these remarks I do not intend to dwell in any great detail or at any length on the historical background to the present Alaska-Canada boundary arrangements. There is no point in reviving ancient and largely buried animosities or opening up old wounds. But certain relevant facts of history should be pointed out for the sake of a wider and better understanding of the problem and of possible remedies or solutions.
In 1825, years before the United States acquired any interest or ownership of the territory of Alaska, Britain and Russia entered into a treaty at St. Petersburg. This agreement defined the boundaries of their respective lands in northwest America.


Canada succeeded to Britain's claims and, in 1867, the United States succeeded to Russia's position through purchase of Alaska.
Section 6 of the 1825 treaty stated in part as follows:
It is understood that the subjects of His Britannic Majesty, from whatever quarter they may arrive, whether from the ocean, or from the interior of the continent, shall forever enjoy the right of navigating freely, and without any hindrance whatever, all the rivers and streams which, in their course towards the Pacific ocean, may cross the line of demarcation upon the line of coast described in article 3 of the present convention.
From time to time minor incidents arose to emphasize the need of a definite interpretation and application of this agreement, but in those days settlers were few and governments busy. Matters drifted until the Klondike discoveries compelled action. Negotiations commenced for such a settlement, but the status of Canada at the time was still that of a colony and London, England, handled negotiations with Washington, D.C., leading up to the appointment of the much-discussed and soundly-cussed Alaska boundary commission and its award in 1903.
Some years previously, in 1889 to be exact, Sir John A. Macdonald raised a definite protest against the United States occupation of territory bordering on the Lynn canal, a large and important inlet in the panhandle between Juneau and Skagway, Alaska. In those days the British foreign office disapproved of communications direct from Ottawa to Washington. So Sir John had Sir Charles Tupper ask the British foreign secretary to instruct the British minister to the United States to convey to the United States state department the protest over the Lynn canal action. The British minister, Sir Lionel Sackville-West, writing from a comfortable summer hotel veranda, informed the state department that some Canadians had raised some objection to some action of Americans about a charter somewhere in the Alaska region, to which the Americans naturally replied it was not so, and there the matter ended.
One good result, at least, that came of the unhappy Alaska boundary negotiations and award was a renewed determination by Canada to do its own negotiating with other nations. However, at the time of the appointment of the Alaska boundary commission, most opinions coincided with that of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, namely, "that there was as much chance of convincing a tribunal, so constituted, of the soundness of the Canadian case as there was of a thaw in Hades."
Since the boundary award, national tempers have cooled and some of the local

pressures declined with lessening activity in the Yukon goldfields. But history has a habit of repeating itself. Once again we find widespread active interest in the natural resources of the northwest and once more there is a growing demand for free access by Canadians to port facilities on the Pacific coast.
In denying such access to Canadians in 1903, the boundary commission probably did not foresee that such denial would retard development of southern Alaska, as well as northwest Canada.
In a brief prepared for the Gordon royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, and dated at Vancouver, December 1, 1955, the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines declared:
It is strongly recommended that the Canadian government should approach the government of the United States to arrange a series of meetings to discuss this vitally important problem. Existence of the foreign-owned strip of land covering the northern coastline of British Columbia is restricting development of mineral resources in the northern section of the province and in the Yukon. It is very obvious the situation will become more aggravated as the north country develops, and becomes of greater importance. Consequently we consider that now is the time for Canada and the United States to get together and discuss, on the usual friendly basis that exists between these two important countries, the matter of arriving at a permanent solution to this problem. "Corridors" through the Alaska panhandle must be established if we are to bring about full development of mineral and other resources in northern areas.
Actually, back in November 1953, the executive committee of the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines had passed a resolution favouring a meeting at an early date between appropriate officials representing the province of British Columbia, the Yukon Territory and the territory of Alaska, to discuss the proposal that the territory of Alaska allow British Columbia and the Yukon access to the ocean by way of a number of narrow strips of land or corridors, cutting through the panhandle of Alaska, so that Canada can develop its own deep-sea ports and industries in these northern areas, which in no way should interfere with the rights of the people of Alaska or with existing terms, ports and other important settlements already established in that territory. It is felt that the establishment of these Canadian ports and subsequent development of hydro electric, mineral and other resources, will bring prosperity to all citizens of Canada and the United States living in those northern areas.
Again in May 1954, Mr. Frank Woodside, manager of the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines, writing to Hon. Hugh Butler, United States senator from Nebraska, and at the time chairman of the United States senate committee on interior and insular
The Budget-Mr. Simmons affairs, stated that the establishment of corridors will eliminate the nuisance of customs inspections, both coming in and going out- and the transferring of men and supplies- so that Canadian mine operators will not be subjected to United States and Canadian regulations in the free operation of their mining properties which, in a few years, will be very extensive.
That letter had followed a speech made in the United State senate on January 29, 1954, by Senator Butler. In his concluding remarks on that occasion, Senator Butler said:
Before I close, these is one problem troubling many Canadians on which I believe we could properly be of help to Canada. That is the question of Canadian access to the Pacific ocean across the Alaska panhandle. It happens that the Alaska panhandle extends down the coast, cutting off Canada's access to the sea as far down as 54 degrees north latitude. That is an unusual situation which might well give rise to conflict and bitterness between any two nations not on friendly terms with each other. Every member of the senate is familiar with the problems that have arisen in European history when a nation has found its access to the sea controlled by another, unfriendly nation. Certainly, no American would be disposed to take advantage of Canada merely because of our strategic position preventing he? access to the ocean. It is a situation where I feel we have a positive obligation to be sympathetic and generous to Canada's need. I am not sure just what kind of an arrangement Canadians might desire. It occurs to me, for example, that we might grant Canada one or more free ports at points along the Alaska coast. I can see no objection to such an arrangement. I do not believe we would consider permanently alienating any American territory to Canadian sovereignty. It is my feeling that both Alaska and the Canadian northwest offer a tremendous frontier for future development. Certainly the industrial development of Alaska should be a definite policy of our governments. I do not believe either Alaska or the Canadian northwest can be fully developed without the closest kind of co-operation between our two nations. I hope the appropriate officials of our government will give serious consideration to these problems so that we can proceed toward joint development of such projects with Canadians to the mutual benefit of both our countries.
It is on that theme and in that spirit that I ask the Minister of External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) now, without delay, to open negotiations with the United States government and with the government of British Columbia leading to a conference between their representatives and representatives of the Canadian government, and of the Yukon Territory and the territory of Alaska, to arrive at a permanent solution to this important and pressing international problem. And I believe it to be essential that the conference be composed of men familiar with the conditions in the area of the panhandle and the whole northwest.
There are several possible solutions and there are important individuals and organizations both in Canada and the United States
2856	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Simmons studying this situation and anxious to find a workable, feasible answer.
For example, United States Senator Richard L. Neuberger, in New Liberty magazine in May 1953, contributed an article on this problem entitled "Let's Swap!" His proposal was that Alaska cede to Canada the port of Skagway, Alaska, and a corridor extending for 21 miles along the White pass and Yukon railway to the boundary with Canada. In return, he suggested Alaska might receive a 119-mile strip bordering the Haines cut-off road through British Columbia and Yukon territory to give Americans access to the Alaska highway from Haines, Alaska, on tidewater.
Possibly a straight exchange of territories is the best answer. It presents some formidable difficulties, however. I lean towards the grant by the United States of strips of land cutting through the panhandle, along with free use of tidewater harbours.
I do not care for the term "corridor" used so much in discussions to date on this problem. The term has unfortunately acquired unhelpful European connotations. Ever since those tense days leading up to world war II the word has become associated in many minds with the idea of conflict and friction. If I may coin a word, I much prefer "accessways" as a description of the sort of 99-year lease or easement arrangement enabling Canadians to travel over portions of the panhandle to freely reach and freely use tidewater port facilities.
I have in mind at least four such accessways: First, traversing the 21 miles from Canadian territory along the White Pass and Yukon railway to Skagway, Alaska; second, from Canada along the Taku river to tidewater at or near the mouth of Taku river; third, from Canada along the Stikine river valley to the mouth of the Stikine river near Wrangell, Alaska; and, fourth, from Pleasant Camp along the Chilkat river valley to Haines, Alaska. None of these United States ports has flourished or prospered as it would do under the proposed plans. They would certainly develop greatly from the increased traffic they would handle from the opening up of the Yukon and northern portions of British Columbia.
I want to stress, Mr. Speaker, that this is not a question of asking favours; it is a matter of two friendly countries seeking a common-sense solution and a method of co-operating for their mutual advantage and benefit. Let us therefore stop fooling around with this problem and let us stop wasting precious time. Let us get an international committee


set up composed of men who know the northwest and know how to get to work with a will.
There are many imposing difficulties, but the problem is not insuperable. It is of interest, for example, to find in the general agreement on tariffs and trade, to which both Canada and the United States are parties, that article 5 on "Freedom of Transit" reads:
1.	Goods (including baggage) and also vessels and other means of transport, shall be deemed to be in transit across the territory of a contracting party when the passage across such territory, with or without trans-shipment, warehousing, breaking bulk, or change in the mode of transport, is only a portion of a complete journey beginning and terminating beyond the frontier of the contracting party across whose territory the traffic passes. Traffic of this nature is termed in this article 'traffic in transit'.
2.	There shall be freedom of transit through the territory of each contracting party, via the routes most convenient for international transit, for traffic in transit to or from the territory of other contracting parties. No destruction shall be made which is based on the flag of vessels, the place or origin, departure, entry, exit or destination, or on any circumstances relating to the ownership of goods, of vessels or of other means of transport.
That gives some idea, Mr. Speaker, of what can be agreed upon as between nations. The difficulties, as I say, are there and cannot be ignored, but as the Alaska Weekly stated in an editorial dated December 4, 1953, if negotiations concerning this problem of accessways are approached in the right spirit, a middle ground certainly will be found upon which agreements can be reached. Too much is at stake for failure on this proposition.
It is very obvious that the situation will become more aggravated as the north country develops and becomes of greater importance. A permanent solution can be made by creating the accessways and it should be done without further delay or inaction on the part of both governments.
The economic strength of Canada and the United States, from which stem our living standards as well as our cultural and material progress, has been a bulwark of the free world. The long period of peace, friendship and happy relations between the two nations represents an achievement and an example to the world.
What has been accomplished fortifies our faith that in this problem I have described today, as in other difficult situations, we can together in the right spirit resolve our differences and difficulties, and march together with mutual benefit and advantage, into the promising future.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I recognize and must state at the outset that the word debate is in itself a misnomer. The word

debate implies either a positive statement or a positive course of action which is the subject or which can be the subject of reasonable and logical discussion. The subject matter which is the subject of this debate is neither positive nor does it go anywhere. It is in fact negative; it is a nullity. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the speech made by the minister and the papers tabled by him are nothing more than nothing and they have been so described from coast to coast. It is a stand-pat and a do-nothing budget which is an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian people.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that no person or group of persons can take any interest in this budget except by way of condemnation unless you perhaps include the tax experts, and I imagine that even they are having their troubles finding very much to chew about. It is, I submit, purely and simply an effort to build a surplus which will be offered back to the long-suffering public one year hence on a silver platter. At that time those who have been slighted this year will be asked to return this machine to power on the basis of its magnanimous and greatly increased tax concessions.
One needs only to read the headlines to realize the effect which this budget has had across the country, an effect which produces only one question and that is: "Well, how much is the surplus going to be next year?"
The minister estimated that he would have a surplus of approximately $100 million and I submit that he based his estimates on present price levels and on a gross national product of $28 billion. I suggest to him that if present trends continue the gross national product will be considerably more than that and the bonanza which this government will have in its hands to deliver to the Canadian public will be considerably greater than the $100 million to which the minister has referred.
As I view the budget, it is designed for the purpose of raising the money that is reasonably necessary to conduct the business of government in an efficient and economical manner. A budget should take a broad view of the whole economy and it should take notice of change in times and conditions. It should be designed not only to permit but also to encourage the development of our natural resources and our industries wherever they may be found. I suggest that this budget cannot be so described by any standard or yardstick. It is purely and simply a ruminative statement which has become so typical of this government, which is content to go along with the stream and,
12, 1956
The Budget-Mr. R. W. Mitchell like a docile child, to reach out and hang on to the coat tails of that beneficent gentleman known as Uncle Sam.
The minister referred somewhat piously to certain weak spots in our economy. At page 2325 of Hansard he is reported as having said, and I quote:
Nevertheless, some sectors of industry and agriculture have not fully shared in this rate of progress.
The minister leaves it there and goes on to a platitudinous discussion of dominion-provincial relations. He does not attempt to deal with, to recognize or to accept any responsibility for the fact that there are weak sectors in our economy. He paid tribute to those who sit on the treasury benches with him. He listened to the plaudits of those who sit around him and keep their toes on the line. He offered nothing in the way of guidance, hope or assistance to the Canadian people. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there has never been such a sham. Never has a budget been so obviously-and I am tempted to say, as the minister interjected during the course of the debate-never has it been "so well used", for purely political purposes.
Much has been said in this house, from all corners of the house, and much has been said and written across this country in recent years on the subject of United States-Cana-dian relations. Public opinion is growing, public opinion is beginning to become conscious, more conscious than ever before, of our birthright. There is a considerably increased demand on the part of Canadians everywhere that we in Canada take a greater responsibility and retain a greater share of control over the development and expansion of our Canadian economy.
There can be no question that capital investment from abroad, particularly from the United States, has contributed greatly to our growth and development in past years. I think in fact that is welcomed by all in every corner of this house. But that is no phenomenon, that is not unusual, that is typical of all young countries struggling to maturity. It was particularly true of the United States itself. It is not so very long ago that the economy of the United States was in fact controlled by the United Kingdom. For a variety of reasons, some of which might be said to be the natural growth and development of the country itself, the natural desire of its people to be masters in their own house and the financial effects on the United Kingdom of two great wars; for these reasons and others, the influence which was formerly so strong has now to all intents and purposes disappeared.

The Budget-Mr. R. W. Mitchell
The same process must take place in Canada and I suggest that that process will take place in two ways. First there will result a change of thinking on the part of citizens of the United States. That change of thinking was very ably and capably stated by the president of the University of Western Ontario, Dr. Hall, at the Boston conference on distribution which met last fall. In order to indicate it I shall quote two short paragraphs from that speech which he entitled "Taking Canada for Granted" and which are as follows:
The real problem, which can be hidden so readily behind the issue of United States capital investment in Canada, is to me not a problem necessarily of dollars and cents. It is a problem of human relations, a problem of respect for others, a problem of philosophy, a problem of understanding and mutual participation. The solution of this problem should not lie in controlling legislation aimed against foreign corporations operating in Canada. It should, I believe, be solved through a major change in the philosophy of "parent corporations" doing business in foreign countries. And specifically in Canada, foreign-owned or foreign-controlled subsidiaries or companies should be listed as Canadian companies, making at least the same type of financial disclosures as do truly Canadian companies, making available to Canadian investors stock in the Canadian subsidiary which reflects only the Canadian operation and making it possible, on the basis of capacity and ability, for top management positions to be filled by Canadians-who know Canada, who love Canada, and whose inherent loyalties are to Canada.
There is no question about the sympathy, understanding, and respect between those from Canada and those from the United States. We are all friends. We believe in the same things. We fight for the same causes. Why then cannot more of the foreign corporations doing business in Canada, making good profits on their Canadian investments, using Canadian materials and labour, selling goods to the Canadian consumer, recognize that the Canadian people not only desire to be, but are becoming determined to be active partners in Canadian enterprises?
With that statement I am in complete agreement. I suggest also that the title of that speech "Taking Canada for Granted" could be well applied to this government. Never have the people of Canada been so taken for granted.
What is the second influence to which I refer? It is an influence which in fact arises out of the remarks made by Dr. Hall. It is an influence which is on the conscience of each and every one of us. We read headlines in the papers such as "How Should we Work for Prosperity, by Selling off Assets to Foreign Investors" or "Dependence on U.S. Goes on Growing". Those are not isolated headlines, they are on the lips of Canadians from one coast to the other. Surely it lies within the realm of this government, and I would hope it would be by way of friendly conference rather than unilateral action, to make sure or at least to take steps to retain control
[Mr. Mitchell (London) .1

and obtain control to a greater extent of our own economy than is presently the case.
I need only refer to a summary of Canada's foreign investment position which appeared in the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin for Friday, April 6, the fourth paragraph of which reads as follows:
The importance of foreign capital to Canadian development has been an outstanding characteristic of Canadian economic history. In turn Canadian development has been a leading influence on the form and course which non-resident investments have taken. The report shows that much of this growth has recently been occurring in investments in Canadian equities which in many cases are accompanied by control. There has been a particularly notable rise in foreign-controlled concerns during the recent period of accelerated development in Canada.
I do not propose to refer to the pipe line except to suggest that that is a typical case, not only of selling out to foreign investors but of actually subsidizing foreign investments in order to enable them to develop and deliver one of our major national resources.
This government has to some extent recognized the problem to which I refer. At page 2332 of Hansard the minister dealt with the problem of Canadian subsidiaries of foreign companies. As is well known, United States firms pay a withholding tax of 15 per cent on dividends unless they are more than 95 per cent owned by the United States parent companies. If there is a minority interest of 5 per cent or less the withholding tax is only 5 per cent. In the case of other countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Eire, to which the minister referred, the preferred rate of 5 per cent on dividends applies if there is more than 50 per cent ownership in the Canadian company. There are other anomalies of a similar nature which were referred to yesterday. One case is the presentation by J. Grant Glassco to the Gordon commission in which he pointed out, and I quote:
There is a marked increase in foreign firms operating here without incorporating Canadian subsidiaries.
In some of these cases they are in fact carrying on their entire business in Canada. The profits so earned by this portion of corporations are dealt with in exactly the same way as Canadian corporations, and there is no withholding tax on the export of the dividends received.
Another problem that has been brought to light recently has to do with restrictions placed by United States corporations on exports by their Canadian subsidiaries. That problem was pointed up in the fall edition of the Business Quarterly, published by the University of Western Ontario school of business administration, in an article written by Mr. Eric Curwain. He said:
One of the most harmful restrictions imposed by U.S. parent companies is that of limiting the

exports of their Canadian subsidiaries to commonwealth countries, and this is now a common practice. When this measure was first put into effect there was in some cases very little disadvantage to the Canadian branch. Now, however, with dollar restrictions imposed on commonwealth buyers, and with the dividing of the world into hard and soft currency blocks, this limitation on Canadian exporters is a big blow to our economy. In making a survey of export potential, the most frequent and disheartening phase heard is: "We export to the commonwealth only-the rest of the world is looked after by our U S. factory." This reply comes from firms engaged in all types of manufacture. It reminds one of the couplet that was alleged to have been sung by humble villagers in England:
God bless the Squire and his relations
And keep us in our proper stations.
That couplet, I might say, seems to be fairly typical of the attitude which this government has taken towards the United States. These incidents are only some of the reasons for our problem. We are, in fact, encouraging minority participation in Canadian subsidiaries of United States firms. We should be going all out to invite those firms to come in on a proper withholding tax basis and thereby not only to permit them to accept Canadian investment but to invite their acceptance of Canadian investment.
All of us here in this house and elsewhere believe that Canada is on the threshold of one of the greatest developments of any country in modern times. However, it is most necessary that we remind ourselves that we are the trustees of it, and it behooves us not to permit this country to become a vassal state of any foreign power, no matter how friendly that power may be.
I submit that, with the increased understanding to which Dr. Hall referred, and of which I am certain there is going to be more, and with legislation to encourage rather than discourage Canadian investment, United States domination will wane. In the result, I suggest that a solution can be reached which will be mutually satisfactory not only to us Canadians, who wish to be the masters in our house, but also to the United States investors of the past and the present, whose assistance we have greatly appreciated and will continue to appreciate.
I now turn to what I would describe as the second crime of omission. It is a crime of omission which this self-satisfied and reluctant dragon has perpetrated in that apparently it considers its only duty to the Canadian people is to follow the lead of someone else or some other government. It does not encourage or offer the facilities for initiative and foresight which from our very inception have been the trademark of Canadianism.
I refer once again to the lack of interest displayed by the minister in the weak spots
The Budget-Mr. R. W. Mitchell of our economy, both industry-wise and area-wise. He said that they have not fully shared in the rate of progress. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. That there are weak links in our economy is indisputable. That nothing has been done about it, that they have not been forcefully dealt with, is undeniable. Apparently the government in its wisdom felt that the wheat farmer represented one of the weak links in our economy. Whilst I do not and cannot agree with the action that it took, I must at least admit that it did take some action. But now once again, having roused itself for one blustering moment, it has relapsed into its usual lethargic state and apparently is ignoring all the other problems with which this country is faced. I can only remind the minister of the warning contained in the brief filed with him on January 31 by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, wherein it is stated:
We are beginning the second decade of the postwar period and it is probable that conditions will differ considerably from what we have come to expect in the past ten years. That the atmosphere will be more competitive can probably be taken for granted. That the rate of technological progress will be even more rapid appears very likely. That there will be less inflation than in the past decade seems likely also, though we are starting off with a reminder that the forces of inflation can with some encouragement become quite active.
If the atmosphere is less inflationary and more competitive, our economy will be less able to shoulder the burden of high taxes. In an atmosphere of rising prices and rapid expansion, levels of taxation which would before the war have been regarded as impossibly high have appeared to have few serious consequences. Yet in a less expansive environment the consequences might well become serious. A young country dependent on enterprise and capital investment for its development can ill afford the kind of deadening of initiative and lack of adaptability which has been associated with unduly high taxation in other times and places. And this conclusion applies with special force in an environment of rapid technological progress where keeping up in the competitive race requires heavy capital investment and the willingness and ability to accept substantial risks.
Yet what has been done? Absolutely nothing. In a previous session of this parliament I referred to the problems which were confronting the textile industry and I suggested that perhaps there should be some changes in the stamping regulations and that they should be more effectively and efficiently enforced. With respect to the same industry, I referred also to certain inequities which had resulted from changing times, higher prices and higher costs. I do not attempt to take any credit for the fact that the government has taken some steps with respect to the stamping regulations which have in part met the problem. It has also resulted in an increased consciousness on the part of the Canadian people that it is good business to buy Canadian.
2860	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. R. W. Mitchell
There are steps that can be taken to assist areas and industries that are in trouble, steps which may involve that hated word "protection". Many briefs have been submitted, many articles have been written and many words have been spoken on this subject. Some recommend that major changes in policy are required; others suggest purely administrative changes to meet the problem. All confirm that we have not been keeping our policy up with the times.
In the present budget speech the minister, as usual, has made a typically timid approach to the problem. To say that we should reconsider tariff policies and tariff structures is not to say that we should immediately build cement walls around the boundaries of this country. Tariffs are living things. Tariffs require change with the times. To say that we should reconsider our tariffs is purely and simply to say that we should view the situation realistically, that we should view it on a broad consistent basis and not on the hit and miss basis with which the government has attempted to deal with the problem.
In referring, Mr. Speaker, to this sinful word, "tariff", I simply wish to put it that this word has been with us for many years, and I suggest that if we look around at some other countries with whom we deal we are going to realize here and now that this selfsame word is going to be with us for many years to come. One of the most horrible examples of the improper use of protection has to do with the 20 per cent tax on advertizing in Canadian issues of United States magazines. I do not intend to refer to that matter in any detail except to say that it is not only discriminatory in its worst sense but it will not accomplish the purpose which the minister predicted it would.
If we have a greater need for protection for our reading public, surely to goodness what we need to do is clear away some of the trash from our newstands which all of us see there in such a flood. Whether or not we like protection, whether or not we agree that all tariffs should be removed, we must not discriminate and we must accept the fact that the nations with whom we are trading have tariffs. We have been recognized as having one of the freest markets in the world and as a result we are getting the worst of the bargain. We are not selling abroad and we are permitting exporters from low cost countries and from some high cost countries to flood our market and disrupt areas and industries which are our first concern. It is high time that we took some positive, concerted action to retain a larger 

percentage of the Canadian marxet for Canadian products. As I said previously, Mr. Speaker, and now reiterate for purposes of emphasis, we have been going at this for too long on a hit and miss basis. Let us get back to the basic concept that our first duty, sitting here as members in this house, is not to the foreign exporter but to the Canadian producer and the Canadian worker.
To turn to another subject briefly, the minister has now had some experience of the result of minor tax concessions. He made certain predictions last year as to the amount of the gross national product. He based his predictions after having taken into account the minor tax concessions to which I have referred, and he missed the mark because, as he himself pointed out, the gross national product was greater than he had bargained for. I am surprised that he did not learn his lesson. If we Canadians desire, and I am satisfied that we do, to take our full share in the development of this country we have got to make money available for expansion and development, and there are only two ways in which that can be done. One is a reduction of taxes and the other is to exert greater economies in the business of government.
I wish to refer to another short paragraph in the same brief. They point out that if our business is to expand we must get away from the high cost economy which we have had, and must put more money back into the hands of the taxpayers. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that with a reduction in taxes this year rather than next year, which will perhaps be more politically expedient, the same results could be obtained by the minister as he purports to obtain in this present session. There are several places in which taxes could be reduced. I do not presume to tell the minister in what way it should be done. One would be a reduction in corporation taxes which would place in the hands of corporations money with which to expand. Another would be to reduce income taxes which would place in the hands of the people the ability to increase our expansion and development. Perhaps the fairest way would be to reduce the sales tax which would have approximately the same result. Any one of these ways would help the weak spots in our economy.
Finally, I simply wish to point out what is the biggest problem of the Canadian people at the moment, one which we have not been able to solve for some time. The biggest problem is to get the government to tackle the problem realistically rather than to keep nibbling at it like a rabbit.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the strictures passed upon the present budget by the last speaker, in which, of course, he was simply ringing variations on the criticisms put forward by various other opposition speakers who have taken part in the debate, it occurred to me that it was just about a year ago that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), who was then practically a newcomer to the responsible and onerous position he holds, brought down his first budget in the house. In listening to many of these criticisms it seems to me that, making allowances of course for the inevitable great differences in detail, there is a general undercurrent of similarity between all the criticisms being offered this year and those put forward last year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is still the same poor government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has been said this year that the budget did not do enough, that the minister did not use the budget effectively as an instrument for the benefit of the Canadian economy and that it was not adapted to the times. Those were the criticisms of a year ago. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that at the present time very few people believe that last year's budget was not ideally suited to the conditions which it had to meet. It is surprising how quickly those criticisms evaporated last year, and I am going to predict that the criticisms of the present budget being put forward this year-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will be overcome next year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-will evaporate just as quickly as did those of last year. Today, with the budgetary emphasis shifted from the need to stimulate to the need to stabilize, I think we will find that the present budget is going to do exactly what it' was intended to do, that it is going to give that steadying touch which is required to enable our economy to roll forward at a satisfactory speed without acquiring the headlong and what would ultimately be the disastrous momentum of uncontrolled inflation.
Most of the speakers in this debate have quoted at length from various publications in support of opinions. I do not' intend to quote anything at length, but I did find what I consider fairly expert confirmation of my opinions about the budget in the columns of the Financial Times. That is a paper which, as far as my observation runs, is not unduly addicted to praise of any kind of this government. The other day some speaker referred, I believe, to an article which had appeared in the same paper concerning the budget. I think it was by Tempus. This is another writer with whom I am concerned and I am
The Budget-Mr. Lusby just going to quote what' his headline says: "The Budget Stands Pat as it Should at the Present Time". That article did not share the view that seems to be so widely held by members of the opposition that a budget is necessarily unsound because it does not bring about any marked change in the tax structure. There is in that article another thing that I might mention and that is that it stated that the present government party in Canada has been lucky in its finance ministers for many years now. I think that there, Mr. Speaker, we have a recognition of the level-headed and sensible manner in which the present minister, like his immediate predecessors, approached the annual problem of the budget. Iri his hands it is a financial instrument which I think is being wielded with skill for the protection of our national economy. On that instrument, it is true, he could have played a more popular tune. Tax reductions are always sweet music.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some critics to my left, oddly enough, seem to construe out of the fact that there are no tax reductions this year, some sinister political motive. I should like to ask those gentlemen, Mr. Speaker, this question. If there had been sweeping tax reductions, would they have said there was no political motive in this action? I think not. It seems to me that if the minister had wished to play politics in this matter, he would have brought down tax reductions. It is all very well to say "Save them for next year". He could give some now and some next year if he wished to do so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did wish to.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the minister would have been delighted, both personally and politically, to have brought down some tax reductions this year if the situation had warranted it. Certainly there is no easier path to popularity. But between the dual necessities of stabilizing the economy and providing the necessary revenues, the situation did not warrant it. That, apart from all else, is demonstrated by the vast defence expenditures which we must continue to incur during 1956. At times during the past year it has seemed that perhaps the longed-for improvement in relations between the communist and non-communist world was approaching with its attendant prospect of a stable peace. But with the failure of the Geneva conference; the vicious and historically false verbal attack by Khrushchev on Britain and the United States during his tour of India, Pakistan and Burma; and the only too evident intention of the
2862	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Lusby U.S.S.R. to foment trouble in the Middle East and in Africa-in the face of such things as those-we have had to lay aside for the time being at least any hope that a stable peace is near.
Such doves of peace as are from time to time sent out from the somewhat leaky, though still seaworthy, ark of the United Nations can as yet find no secure resting place for the soles of their feet. While that ark floats we need not despair but, Mr. Speaker, at the present time there is no room for any substantial curtailment in our defence effort.
Some see brighter prospects for peace in the recent apparent repudiation in the U.S.S.R. of one-man dictatorship as exemplified' by the late and now universally unlamented Joseph Stalin, the apparent discrediting of one-man dictatorship in favour of rule by a group, even such a group as now appears to be in control in the Kremlin. I do not share any optimism in that regard. For the time being, it is true, junta rule seems to be the order of things in the U.S.S.R., and I think perhaps it is true to say that generally group or collective leadership may be expected to show at least some elements of moderation and caution. Perhaps this has had a considerable bearing upon the adoption of the present Kremlin policy of continuing the world struggle without manifest aggression.
But it seems to me that rule by a group, large or small, is not a natural, and is unlikely to be an enduring, attribute of any totalitarian state. Sooner or later the strong man, the authentic dictator-"tyrant" is a more forthright word-emerges, in whom, as supreme head, all real power is concentrated. The rule of several is replaced by the rule of one. Collective leadership resolves itself into the collecting by the strong man of the scalps of the other leaders. This is, I suggest, a general lesson of history in respect of junta rule, from Julius Caesar to Napoleon and even later. It is my growing belief that in Nikita Khrushchev, first secretary of the communist party, we have the future tyrant of Russia, absolute and merciless, the very avatar of that Joseph Stalin whom he now so bitterly denounces. If any one man is to emerge supreme from that group of Russian leaders-and one inevitably will-surely it is Khrushchev, the strongest and most malignant of them all.
How far the process of Khrushchev's aggrandizement has already gone it may be difficult to gauge, but certainly he is far on the climb to the summit. Although he has not yet thrown off the constitutional cloak-perhaps he may never need to do so-it is significant that the congress of the communist 

party in Moscow, in addition to re-electing Khrushchev as first secretary, recently added 53 new members, all known supporters of his, to the central committee which in turn re-elected, without change, the Praesidium, the supreme ruling group of eleven, including Khrushchev. The latter's elevation to the leadership of the committee which controls the Russian federation, most important of the republics of the Soviet union, is yet another indication that he is augmenting and consolidating his power.
When the process is complete, the group replaced by one man, and he such as I conceive Khrushchev to be, with absolute mastery of a mighty state, moderation and caution are likely to be set aside in favour of a policy of active armed aggression. This, too, is a lesson of history; sooner or later the tyrant, to bolster his own position, embarks or is driven to embark upon a career of foreign conquest by force of arms, even as Hitler did.
I do not suggest that today's strong man would court such a war as would call down a mutual rain of hydrogen bombs with its likelihood of utter destruction for either side. But I do suggest that his probable choice would be an unending series of localized conflicts, similar to that which we faced in Korea. Certainly we know to our sorrow that the opportunities to precipitate such conflicts in the world today are extremely numerous; and such a policy carries but little danger that the west would resort to the H-bomb so long as it appeared that our opponents did not intend to do so.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the ominous shadow of the rising Khrushchev, we must maintain our conventional arms at a high level, whatever the budgetary or other burden entailed may be. It is true that the hydrogen bomb must continue to be our ultimate defence. But it is not a weapon adapted to meet all situations any more than dynamite is suitable to destroy rats in a cellar.
If we wished to use a slogan by which our national defence policy and our international policy should be guided at the present time, I think we could put it in three words: Khrushchev means mischief.
To the burden of arms must be added, as an essential means of combating the spread of communism, the extension of assistance to raise the standards of living, health and education in the impoverished countries of the world. Here the United Nations, through its many programs directed towards that end, renders inestimable service. But at this time I should like to emphasize rather the value of the Colombo plan as representing one of the finest opportunities we have to block the

growth of communist influence in fellow countries of the commonwealth. This government is greatly to be commended for its decision to increase Canadian participation in the Colombo plan. That is a decision which I strongly endorse.
I know that some Canadians, even many who fully approve our armament program, find it difficult to understand why we should spend large sums abroad for the economic benefit of other countries. I am glad to note, however, that there seems to be a steadily growing public appreciation of the value of such expenditures, both as a humanitarian measure and as a component of our national security. Both in conversations and in correspondence I have in recent months received from responsible and well-informed Canadian citizens-at least I consider them so-more and more expressions of approval of the Colombo plan and of our increasing participation in it. I am glad, Mr. Speaker, to bring this to the attention of the house at this time.
In touching upon matters of external and international import, Mr. Speaker, I do not forget that in any balanced program of government, internal and domestic affairs must bulk large. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) stated in his budget address, the past year has been for Canada one of marked economic progress and expansion. But all sections of our economy have not shared equally in the advance, and this government can play no more important part than to endeavour within its own sphere, and with the means at its command, to redress any inequities thereby resulting.
I have often urged, in this house and elsewhere, the need to rectify the regional inequalities which exist in our economy, particularly with respect to the maritime provinces. But there are occupational as well as regional inequalities, and it sometimes happens that the two coincide, with a resulting double effect.
At this session of the house no subject, I think, has received more attention than the state of our agricultural industry. Fundamental though its prosperity is to the economic well-being of this country, it has fallen behind as compared with some other industries. If our present era of progress and expansion is to continue on a permanent basis, the farmer must be ensured his fair share of the national income. It happens that the province of Nova Scotia, with which I of course am more particularly concerned, was one of three in which farm income showed an increase during the past year; but nonetheless it is clear, even to those of us who cannot and do not pose as agricultural
The Budget-Mr. Lusby experts, that the farmer today, in Nova Scotia as elsewhere in Canada and, indeed, in most countries of the western world, has among his problems two which are fundamental. The problem is not peculiar to us. First, he must find sufficient markets for his products. Second, the prices he receives for those products must bear a reasonably favourable ratio to his cost of producing them. In short, prosperity for the farming industry, as in every other, is dependent upon being able to sell and to sell at a profit. That, you say, is obvious, and it is; and yet the solution for the farmer is not at all obvious under present conditions. But unless a solution is found the agricultural industry will not hold a position of reasonable prosperity in our economic structure. If it fails to do so we might liken the result to the crumbling of a foundation stone which will ultimately bring down the whole structure.
There has been no paucity of suggested remedies, Mr. Speaker, for the problem of farm markets and that of the unfavourable price-cost relationship in agriculture, and I certainly do not consider myself competent to advance any complicated remedies of my own. I rather wish just to bring the situation once more to the attention of the house. There is, however, one detail which may be comparatively minor, but which I think is not entirely unimportant, and which I should like to mention at this time. In my opinion, insufficient attention is being paid to the very definite shift in consumer preference in the matter of foodstuffs which is noticeably taking place.
Earlier in this session I heard the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) fulminating against what he described as "rabbit food". Whatever the merit of his criticism may have been, I think it is true that a trend away from certain of our more substantial staple foods toward lighter foods has definitely set in, which neither this house nor any member of it can halt. As the machine increasingly supplants human muscle for the performance of heavy work, we might expect this trend to accelerate. And it seems to me that much more attention and research might profitably be paid to efforts to chart the probable course of this trend so as to forecast as accurately as can be done for the farmer the type of foodstuffs for which he may best hope to find an expanding market in the future.
There are, of course, many staple foods which show no decline in popularity. There is, for example, every indication that beef will continue in high favour with the eating public. I doubt whether many of us can find in
2864	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Lusby our appetites that there has yet been discovered any satisfactory substitute for a roast of beef or a good steak. I think there is no more promising avenue for agricultural progress in my province of Nova Scotia than the raising of beef cattle.
It is the view which has been expressed by officials of our provincial department of agriculture. They say that success of agriculture in Nova Scotia in the coming years will depend to a considerable degree upon the development of the livestock industry. And when we reflect that Nova Scotia imports something like $18 million worth of meat annually, it is evident that room exists for a marked expansion of beef-raising in the province as well as the production of other meats.
As the great marshlands reclamation project proceeds, thousands of fertile acres have become available for use, and they can be put to no better use, in my opinion, than the raising of beef. There is no doubt that they can sustain a large population of cattle. Many years ago beef-raising on the marshes was a profitable and important pursuit and today in various areas considerable progress has already been made again in this direction. There are certain problems which remain to be fully solved; one notable one is that of caring for the maximum number of cattle with a reasonable minimum of labour.
The dominion experimental farm at Nap-pan, on the fringe of the marshlands in my constituency, has devoted a great deal of attention to the solving of these problems, and has achieved, I would say, a very considerable degree of success. I should like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that such research and experimentation in this regard should be pursued with the utmost vigour. The promotion of a beef-raising industry on the marshlands ought to be considered a natural and integrated extension of the vast marshlands project itself, in which this government has played so leading a part. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, it is my view that a great deal more could be done to educate those farmers who own marshlands and who might, with the proper guidance, develop a very large beef-raising industry on those marshlands.
With regard to the disparity between farm prices and cost of production-I am leaving aside the question of any direct governmental intervention in the matter of prices-it is evident that any advance in the efficiency of farm operation which lowers the cost of production without increasing the amount of such production would tend to ease the problem. In this connection, it is my view, Mr. Speaker, that in many parts of the country there is much marginal and submarginal land now
[Mr. Lusby.1

unprofitably devoted to agricultural purposes which might better be turned to other uses, thereby increasing farming efficiency generally and lowering costs of production. I have in mind not so much poor or worn-out lands which might be built up for better agricultural use in the future. That is what I think the United States soil bank plan primarily envisages. But I have in mind rather lands which by their nature will never be well suited to efficient agricultural operations in a fiercely competitive era such as this one undoubtedly is.
In my province, the alternative to using such lands for agriculture, generally speaking, would be to let them revert to the growing of timber, which has a relatively rapid growth in the maritime provinces. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it would be worth while to consider the feasibility of some joint provincial-federal plan of action whereby provision might be made to encourage the extensive diversion of such lands as I mention to reforestation. Although timber resources and reforestation projects are primarily matters of provincial concern, I do not think anyone would deny that today the state of our agricultural industry is a matter of national concern. A plan of action such as I have suggested for consideration would serve a dual purpose, not only promoting the efficiency of agricultural production generally but also, in the long view, adding to those forest reserves which are going to be of steadily increasing value and importance in our future economic life.
This government has already done much, of course, to better the position of our agricultural industry. I welcome those tariff and other changes effected by the present budget which have as their aim the improvement of the farmer's position. The assistance of the movement of feed grains from west to east has been of incalculable benefit to eastern farmers and I urge that this be raised to the level of a fixed national policy.
The price support program for butter has similarly benefited the dairy industry, and in my opinion the recent decision to extend the program for two years is a wise and sound one. None the less, it seems to me that price support for any particular commodity is a temporary rather than a permanent solution. In the United States a general policy of agricultural price support, by leading to the accumulation of enormous surpluses, threatens in the end to injure rather than aid the farming industry.
A long term solution for the agricultural problems of Canada, as I said earlier, depends upon encouraging the utmost efficiency of farm production without at the same time

increasing that production beyond the bounds of available markets. The problem is complicated by the need to preserve the independence and individuality of the small farmer. Here a greater degree of co-operative action among the small farmers themselves might well be encouraged; but whatever the best solution may prove to be, the problem of maintaining a reasonable degree of agricultural prosperity calls for the best efforts of all governments in this country.
A rapid increase in our national population, by promoting larger domestic consumption of foodstuffs, would go far toward solving the marketing problems which the Canadian farmer faces. Such an increase in population, of course, is closely linked to the continuance of the general economic expansion in this country which the policies of this government have done so much to foster.
The official opposition has of late been decrying the influx of United States capital into this country. The previous speaker devoted some time to this subject. In some respects I was able to agree with him but not in all respects. Vast capital expenditures are necessary to maintain the rapid pace of our Canadian development and it is obvious that only a part of the funds required can be supplied from Canadian sources. As an ideal, I grant that Canadian development through Canadian investment only has much to commend it, but I certainly do not think we should allow the economic development of this country to lag for a generation or two awaiting a sufficiency of Canadian capital for that development. I think that mine is the view of the Canadian people as a whole.
Looking to the future, I do not fear undue United States dominance of our economic life and resources. As the previous speaker mentioned, we are passing through a phase which I think is experienced by every young richly dowered, expanding, and relatively undeveloped country, when an influx of outside capital is essential for the full realization of its economic potentialities. At one time the United States itself was largely dependent upon English capital to speed its development, and no doubt many shortsighted fears were expressed concerning the dangers of British economic dominance.
I have no doubt that, as our population and national wealth increase we shall emerge from that stage even as the United States did. I do not think the solution is to endeavour to put impediments in the way of United States investments in this country. We should always remember that largely because of its stable government Canada is perhaps the most promising field for foreign investment in the world today. But it is not the only field. I would ask hon. members of the opposition to
The Budget-Mr. Jones consider the possibilities of South America, which is also a young, richly dowered, expanding and relatively undeveloped continent. It is quite reasonable to suppose that if it achieved stable government it would be very easy for the stream of United States investment to be turned from the north to the south and in time it would detract from the stream of United States investment in this country. To hamper United States investment in Canada and to make United States investors second-class investors might easily lead to the drying up of the stream of United States investment to Canada, and I think that would put Canada at a great disadvantage.
