speechtext: They have already tried it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the meantime 1 think we should let United States capital come in because, as I said, I have no fears concerning the future of this country. As our wealth increases I am convinced that we will eventually assume the proper control, the overwhelming control, of all our economic life. I do not think that to attempt to hamper United States investment at this time is a remedy. I believe that foreign investments generally, from the United States and elsewhere, will lead to the speedy achievement of the full national and economic stature which is our destiny. Mr. Speaker, let us achieve it in our time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like for a brief while to discuss one aspect of the budget that has been touched upon only lightly but which to me is of extreme importance. Like many other hon. members, I was very disappointed to find that the budget provided no relief for the municipalities. This disappointment was also expressed by people I met during my recent visit to British Columbia. During the time I am on my feet I hope to try and pass on to the government the thoughts that were expressed to me concerning this dissatisfaction.
To my personal knowledge the municipalities have been trying hard to penetrate the iron curtain surrounding this government as they have tried to do for many years through their reeves, mayors, organizations, delegations and resolutions. They have tried in every way to approach the government as an equal governing body, but so far, despite the fact that they attended one of the dominion-provincial conventions, they were brushed aside and are still not recognized. I therefore feel that someone should speak on their behalf at this time.
The municipalities are faced with mounting costs. Wages and materials have gone up.
2866	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Jones The municipalities have undertaken to take care of 50 per cent of the expenses in connection with civil defence. They also still bear an unfair share of the cost of unemployment which I think should be taken completely out of their hands. They continue to bear an unfair share of the social services, particularly in the rural areas of British Columbia.
On the other side of the picture their limited field of revenue has not been enlarged for generations; it still remains basically the same. Both federal and provincial governments receive the bulk of their income from municipal dwellers. These governments get several times more than the municipalities in the form of revenue. In my estimation income from these sources has increased during the last ten years by several hundred per cent, while the municipalities have been barely able to catch up with the increased costs of their operations. They must derive their income from what is left after the two senior governments are finished.
It has been pointed out to me that there is a limit to this, and many municipalities feel they have reached that limit. I know some are now in the position where they can no longer borrow legally; and therefore they must curtail many of the services that are essential for their welfare and development. The municipalities are faced with two alternatives because of the failure of the federal government to assist them. First, they can increase taxation and assessment within the municipal boundaries, but in many cases this would be unthinkable because taxation is so high at the present time. I do not think any taxpayer would stand for an increase. The other alternative is to reduce many of the services now rendered, but again the taxpayer would not agree.
We in British Columbia are proud of our municipalities, of what they have done, of how they have developed; we are proud of what they have done with regard to the building of new schools, roads, sidewalks; the development of parks, lighting and water systems; the providing of sewerage and social services; the building of hospitals and the way in which they have taken care of unemployment and civil defence. But all this has placed an extra burden upon these municipalities, because in recent years there has not been an increase in the boundary of any British Columbia municipality. Adjoining areas have grown up but they are afraid to come into the municipality because of the tremendously higher costs that would be involved, caused by the burdens I have referred to. So they remain outside of the municipal boundary as long as they can, which is not good for the district or the
fMr. Jones.]

people because it means essential services necessary for a healthy condition of life are not being provided.
Total municipal debt and the interest thereon has increased. Generally speaking the municipalities of British Columbia have been well governed and their resources and finances have been well administered. But in spite of this the over-all debt has been increasing and as a result essential improvements are being delayed, or as I have been told abandoned in some cases. Most of the municipalities in my riding have written urging federal assistance or the acceptance by the federal government of the municipality as an independent taxing body which would not be subject to taxation by a senior body, whether provincial or federal. Of course in this case it is the federal government.
I shall try to outline briefly how the federal government could help the municipalities by recognizing their obligations, inasmuch as the bulk of their revenue comes from that source. They cannot entirely shake off their responsibilities. They could help by becoming responsible property owners. They are now property owners in the municipality, but they are irresponsible property owners because they pay no taxes. Usually the post office or public building is located on the best site in town, and these federal government buildings are provided with fire and police protection, road and sewage services and everything else. They do not even say, "Thank you" by dropping the municipality a line in appreciation of the services they have obtained for nothing during the year.
It is time that they not only thanked the municipalities but assumed their rightful place as taxpayers within the municipality. Certainly the post office makes money out of its operations. I know that most municipalities appreciate what the government has done with regard to the taxation on public buildings, but even the new formula under which we are now operating does not seem to assist a great deal. In answer to a question I asked last month I was informed by the Minister of Finance that the total number of municipalities which have applied for assistance under this formula totalled only 11 per cent. Those municipalities think they have a chance of getting it and presumably most of them will get it, but 89 per cent of the municipalities in this dominion feel they have no claim on the government under the strict formula which has been worked out. It is on behalf of those municipalities which constitute 89 per cent of the total who cannot qualify that I urge the minister to reconsider the present position and have the government become a taxpayer in the true sense of the word in connection with all federally owned property

within municipal boundaries. It would not hurt the government and it would certainly create a nice taste in the mouths of municipal councils across Canada, who I think have good grounds for complaint.
Even with this formula, if the government had kept pace with the growth of our municipalities by building, more municipalities could have qualified; but they have not provided adequate buildings to house the various departments. Instead we find them scattered all over town, located in old stores or upstairs in buildings. In the Okanagan valley we find these departments located mostly in converted stores. It is time the government erected adequate buildings. I know in the case of Vernon one has been promised for many years, but it is still in the promise stage. In the case of Penticton we have been promised that the public building will be finished by 1960, but as yet the land has not been purchased. The building at Kelowna is still under consideration. These three towns happen to be in the district where I live, and I know their needs and circumstances.
There should be public buildings to take care of the various federal government departments. The fact that the municipalities cannot qualify under the formula shows that the public building is valued at a low figure. Otherwise it would not be hard to come within the formula of 2 per cent of the assessment of the municipality. In one case the present building is quite old and I understand it is about to be scrapped.
I urge the minister to abolish the present formula and pay a tax on all government property within municipal limits just as other taxpayers do.
My next suggestion is that the federal sales tax be removed from all municipal purchases, as is done in the case of hospitals. I know that the tax has been removed in the case of some large purchases by municipalities in Canada. In my opinion a sales tax on municipal purchases is unwarranted and unjust. It simply imposes another burden on the already heavily burdened municipal taxpayer. It is imposed in a rather bullying sort of way, in that the one tax-receiving body imposes it on the other tax-receiving body because it is bigger and in a better position to impose its authority.
Two municipalities in my riding, West Summerland and Penticton, operate irrigation systems. Some time ago these municipalities had occasion to buy pipe and other equipment for irrigation works within their municipal limits. On their behalf I applied to the government for a rebate of the sales tax paid on these purchases, but I was flatly turned
The Budget-Mr. Jones down on the ground that such purchases did not come within the provisions of the present act. I feel that when a municipality is prepared to help out its own citizens and its own farmers by providing an irrigation system it should receive a rebate of the sales tax. On behalf of these municipalities I would ask that when the government finally arrives at the point where they will allow a rebate of sales tax to municipalities, they consider including in such rebate provisions, purchases in connection with irrigation projects operated by municipalities.
About a year ago the Minister of Finance intimated that consideration would be given to the reopening of the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act if a desire for that action were expressed by the provincial governments during the federal-provincial convention. That desire was expressed. I understand the premier of British Columbia was one in favour of the proposal, and he told me that the matter would be brought up at that convention. The matter, having been brought up, was cold-shouldered. Nothing was done about it and nothing will foe done because, I understand, the government is not in favour of reopening this act. I am sorry about that, and I hope I am wrong. It would render great assistance to the municipalities if it were reopened.
As I have mentioned before this act, while it was in operation, was very successful, providing 2 per cent money for self-liquidating municipal projects. It helped, as far as British Columbia was concerned, to build up water works, lighting systems and hydroelectric and other types of municipal projects of that kind. We have them to this day, real tangible assets, at very little cost to the dominion government.
The municipalities today are urgently in need of cheap money for similar works, where towns have grown and where new towns have sprung up, and they are unable to get sufficient money owing to the high cost. They would all welcome this act. They have pleaded with me to do what I can to have it reopened. I cannot understand the government's indifference to this, because while it operated they made money. They did not lose money; they made money. Every cent borrowed and every cent of interest has been paid in full, and I think that is a remarkable achievement. On the other side, they can show with pride all the excellent projects that have been completed to the benefit of the Canadian people. Money at 2 per cent, as I point out, would add materially to our tangible assets, and without any financial embarrassment to the government or the municipality.
2868	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Jones
Another way to assist the municipality would be for the federal government to assume all costs resulting from unemployment. At present the municipalities still bear a substantial part of the cost, which I claim should be a federal responsibility, especially as far as British Columbia is concerned, because we have people migrating from every province in Canada to spend a warmer winter in British Columbia, and naturally many become a burden on the municipality. Because of the roving nature of Canada's unemployed, I feel the whole burden should be assumed by the federal government.
Another suggestion I am going to make is with regard to education. The bulk of municipal taxes today is devoured by educational costs. For years and years a desire has been expressed by the municipalities for some form of federal aid. It is difficult to arrive at what form that aid should take, but I am going to suggest that the simplest way would be to make a per capita grant to school districts, where school districts are in existence, or to municipal bodies. It could be done in some other way, but a per capita grant throughout the dominion would help to solve the problem.
Education actually is more of a federal problem than a municipal one. We are all anxious to get an equal standard throughout the whole dominion. One municipality may have a high standard and the next one a low standard, because of its revenue. So the only body that could truly lay claim to being able to have a universal dominion-wide standard would be the federal government. For that reason I think the federal government should step into that field with assistance, and this is a suggestion as to how this equality could be obtained. I believe all Canadians should have equal opportunities, but unfortunately if something is not done to meet the rising cost of education the authorities will be forced to cut down the educational curricula themselves.
I have made these suggestions, realizing that the government of Canada is a team proposition. The team is composed of the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal governments, and each member of that team is entitled to a fair share of the common income. There is only the one common income, what the people of Canada earn from their labour, whether physical or mental. So far the municipalities have been ignored by the senior governments, especially the federal government, and it is time they realized the importance of the junior member of the team and gave it a break. Any or all of the suggestions I have just made could be implemented at little cost to the federal government but


with immense benefit to the municipalities. I trust the minister will give serious consideration to this before it is too late and we have trouble in the municipalities themselves.
There is one other subject I should like to mention; that is the care of our senior citizens. I had a letter from a group in Oliver, British Columbia, the other day. This group is trying to get federal assistance to build a home for senior citizens. The only type of home the government more or less sponsors is the small cottage built under the National Housing Act. These people have a scheme whereby 21 or more old people would live in one large home, which might be called a boarding house. This could be built for approximately $70,000, including accommodation for the staff and everything else. If you take the unit cost of taking care of a senior citizen under this scheme as compared with the unit cost of building a separate home, you will find it is considerably less. The care of senior citizens would be under proper management. In this case in Oliver it would be a co-operative effort by the citizens of the town. There is no means of getting a federal government grant. The provincial government is putting up one-third of the cost, and the suggestion is that the citizens of Oliver put up one-third and the federal government put up the other one-third. I think it is a fair and sound proposition which would benefit the federal government by allowing these people to live in decent circumstances.
Again I suggest the federal government has the responsibility, because many of these people have drifted to British Columbia on attaining the age at which they are eligible for old age pension. They have come there for the same reason that others drift in, for the climate. For the same reason I advanced before, I feel the government has the responsibility to see that these people are properly housed. Here is an opportunity to bear one-third of the cost of a worthy project. If the government would extend the facilities of the National Housing Act, if necessary, or act through some other means to encourage the building of such homes, I am satisfied that other centres in British Columbia would also come into the field of providing homes that are much needed by these older people. Again, in doing so it would help the municipalities which, in the absence of help from the federal government, must put up the difference and bear the cost of operating these homes. Therefore I hope the minister will give consideration to assisting such projects for the senior citizens of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to congratulate the Minister of Finance on the budget he has presented at this session of parliament. A year ago the

minister presented a budget which appeared to some to be too optimistic. However, by reason of the general development of the country and the increase in general business, Canada's gross national product reached a record level.
Before coming into the chamber I had occasion to read the current comment of the celebrated columnist, Mr. Bruce Hutchison. In his article Mr. Hutchison said that just as in the ordinary affairs of man, just as in the affairs of any business corporation, so in the affairs of the nation there is a time to pause and take stock and appraisal of the situation of that particular business or household. He went on to say that if he could read the mind of the Minister of Finance he would say that at this time he was taking that pause to determine Canada's position for the future. This is the second budget presented by the present Minister of Finance. I hope he will bring down further successful budgets as long as he has the honour of holding the portfolio he now holds.
On my return to the Niagara district during the Easter recess I found the fruit and vegetable growers not in any spirit of despair but rather in a spirit of anxiety over the fact that their gross incomes have been reduced below the level of the incomes of those persons who are employed in industry or who are engaged in mercantile or commercial business. They were pleased to know that Canada's economy was at a record high level, but they believed that they were entitled to a greater share of the prosperity at the present time.
In spite of conflicting reports that the rich alluvial fruit lands are being encroached upon by industrial concerns and commercial developments, there are still many fine agricultural acres in the Niagara peninsula to be developed and cultivated. The splendid, mild climate still prevails in that area, and the farmers there are as resourceful as ever. Nevertheless there are several problems which prevent the agriculturists from moving into an equal position with the industrial worker. I am one of those who believe that the agricultural worker, the fruit grower, the vegetable grower and their wives and families should not be asked to accept less for their toil than those who work in commercial business or in industrial pursuits. Every person is entitled to the fruits of his hire.
The problems of the farmer have been fairly accurately set forth in an address delivered by Mr. H. H. Hannam at the twentieth annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held in Hamilton on January 24, 1956. The situation being encountered in this country is not one that is
The Budget-Mr. Cavers peculiar to this country alone. I think the same problems are being met in the United States of America. In his address Mr. Hannam cites the problems of Canadian agriculture, and I can do no better than to quote his summation of the problem, which is in these words:
(a)	Markets are lagging behind farm output.
(b)	All-time high costs of production are being held rigid, or are rising, while farm prices have fallen.
(c)	Comparatively little progress is being made through intergovernmental co-operation in improving international distribution of food and agricultural products.
So far as the first item is concerned, the matter of markets lagging behind farm output, I think it is recognized that our output is far greater than our present consumption. There is a great need for more people in our country to use the great output of agricultural products. An increase in population will bring a greater consumption of our natural farm products. There is also a need, and I think a greater need, to market our farm products in a more attractive manner.
I refer particularly to the fruit and vegetable growers who live in the constituency which I represent. I believe they could dress up their produce in a much better manner than is the case at the present time. We see fruit and vegetables not grown in this country but which are brought here and sold not because their price is any less but because they are packaged in a more attractive container.
I think the formation of producer-controlled marketing boards is vital to the industry. The farmers of my area are not asking for handouts or subsidies. They wish to solve their own marketing and other problems, but they realize they have a need for an orderly program of selling their production. A marketing board or marketing scheme or system will bring with it a sales force for the distribution of natural farm products. It will provide a more adequate method of packaging the product which will appeal to the consumer. It will bring about a uniform high standard of quality over which there can be some supervision. It will also bring with it a medium of public advertising which can be sponsored by the particular marketing board.
But such marketing boards require effective legislation to give legal status to their regulations. In Ontario the farm products marketing act was passed in 1950. It appears in the revised statutes of Ontario, 1950, chapter 131. Subsequent amendments were introduced in the years 1953, 1954 and 1955. However, this legislation has been attacked as being indirect

The Budget-Mr. Cavers taxation and beyond the jurisdiction of a provincial legislature. The constitutional issues are embodied in a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada which will be heard this month.
It is expected that the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada who hear the reference will bring down a judgment some time this spring. If the legislation is held to be within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, then the act will enable the growers in our area to continue the progress they have made during the past year. Should the Supreme Court of Canada find that the legislation is lacking in some manner which can be repaired by a provincial legislature, then I suggest that it is within the scope and jurisdiction of the provincial legislature to provide the remedy in order to make that legislation effective.
But if the provincial legislation is found to be ultra vires or bad in some manner, and it cannot be cured by the provincial legislature, then I believe it would be necessary for this house to provide proper legislation in order to make the provincial legislation effective. In the interests of the fruit and vegetable growers whom I have the honour to represent, the hog producers, the cheese producers and all those persons who are engaged in the distribution of farm products, it seems to me that this course of action is advisable. If it is needed, the federal legislation should be drafted and ready. Delay in presentation, creating a hiatus during the summer months, would cause a serious situation in regard to the realistic marketing of farm products throughout the country.
I said that Mr. Hannam referred to the need for co-operation among interdepartmental agencies in order to improve international distribution of food and agricultural products. Mr. Hannam's words were "little progress is being made". If little progress is being made in this matter, which caused his complaint, I suggest that it is not the fault of the departments of this government.
In the fall of 1953, I felt that some assistance needed to be rendered to the growers of our district. I called together representative fruit and vegetable growers in my district to discuss this very problem. They formed a committee of five members. At the request of this committee an interdepartmental committee comprising representatives of the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance, and the Department of Transport was formed with the help of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture, the then minister of finance and the then minister of transport. These two groups


-on the one hand specialists of the various departments of government and on the other hand practical producers who understood the problems with which they were confronted- came together here in Ottawa to discuss the problems of this industry. I can say, Mr. Speaker, that the results were beneficial and gratifying.
I desire to express the thanks of the fruit and vegetable growers of the Niagara district to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to Mr. Richard Bower and to Mr. Bruce Marshall of his London office for the assistance they gave the growers of our district in getting our fruit and vegetables on the British market in 1954 and 1955. In 1954 the growers of our district sent Mr. W. C. Nickerson, a prominent fruit grower, to Britain. With the assistance of these men whom I have named they were able, working together, to arrange for the sale of our canned fruit and vegetables on the British market. It was a godsend to the growers of our area. They are expecting to continue to send the fine processed fruit and vegetables from our area to the British markets again this year. This effort was only a beginning and in a small way, but it reflects what can be done when a spirit of co-operation exists between the specialists in the various government departments and experienced agriculturists who know the problems with which they are confronted.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture should be complimented on setting up a committee on policy. The committee, headed by Mr. Jack Brodrick, an outstanding and capable agriculturist who resides in the county of Lincoln, have done much to help the agricultural policy of the country. Mr. Brodrick and his associates, after two years of effort, have brought down an eight-section report which, assembled, provides a national policy for Canadian agriculture. It indicates on the part of Canadian farmers a willingness to face their problems and to endeavour to provide a solution for their difficulties. In turn they desire and request the assistance and support of governments, both provincial and federal, to create a favourable climate in which agriculture can work. I am sure that assistance will be forthcoming, and that the lot of the Canadian farmer will be greatly improved, largely because of his own industry and initiative.
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if before I sit down I did not mention one fact. On two occasions I have spoken in the interests of those citizens who are obliged to accept handicaps which we do not know. I refer to the blind citizens of this country. They suffer a great handicap. They bear their burden cheerfully, and in many cases they endeavour

through their own efforts to support themselves and their families. On previous occasions I have requested of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance that the payments made to these blind persons should be made without a means test.
If it is not possible to provide these people with their assistance without a means test, the blind citizens of this country are asking for an additional cost of living allowance to provide for the additional assistance which they require. This includes helpers who must accompany them on trips which they are obliged to take. On many occasions they are obliged to provide themselves with taxis at their own expense. They are asking for a small supplementary payment that would assist them in this way. I am sure that a small payment of this kind to the blind people of this country would not cause too heavy a drain on the public purse, and that it would not provide too much difficulty for the taxpayers of this country. It would certainly be greatly appreciated by those who have difficulty in caring for themselves.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the budget was brought down a short time ago I listened with rapt attention to what the minister had to say, and I must say that I was greatly disappointed when he concluded his address.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was disappointed because several things which I hoped would be in the budget' were not included. I had hoped the minister would be in a position to give us an assurance that there is definite hope that some adjustment in the tariff can be made which will produce a more equitable situation as between the producers of potatoes in Canada and those in the United States. The same thing applies to a new product which holds considerable promise for the fishing industry, namely processed fish sticks. Unfortunately, at the present time Canadian processed fish sticks meet a very high tariff on going into the United States, and the hoped-for benefit to the fishing industry has not as yet materialized.
But a third thing was absent from the minister's remarks, namely a satisfactory recognition of the problems of the maritime provinces at the present time. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is my responsibility to again bring to the attention of the house, to the best of my ability, the difficulties under which the maritime provinces have found themselves for most of the time since they joined confederation.
The Budget-Mr. MacLean
Like the other provinces, the maritime provinces went into confederation on the assumption that they would be equals and would be treated as such. Theoretically, the colonies that joined together to form our present Dominion of Canada looked upon themselves as equals, and in fact they were within reason at least of the same relative importance; they fell roughly within the same category. However, at the present time the maritime provinces find that in fact they are not equal members of an association. That is only a theory. They find instead that they are the little fellows away off at the far end of the Canadian table, and when the platter gets to them they find that the best has been picked over, if not removed entirely. As a matter of fact we find that we are forced to refer to ourselves as the poor relatives in the Canadian family.
I should like to be in a position to congratulate the minister, to exchange some pleasantries and so forth, but owing to the situation in which I find myself I must run the risk of being possibly rather critical, and in any case my remarks may be received with some distaste. It is not because I have any wish to be objectionable; nor is it owing to the fact that any animosity may exist between this party and any other party. It is owing to the fact that we are poor relations, and I am speaking on their behalf at the present time. We have only to refer to Charles Lamb's essay on poor relations to see in what an unenviable position I find myself at the present time. He said:
A poor relation is the most irrelevant thing in nature-a haunting conscience-a preposterous shadow, lengthening in the noontide of our prosperity-an unwelcome reminder-a perpetually recurring mortification-a drain on your purse- a more intolerable dun upon your pride-a drawback upon success-a rebuke to your rising-a stain in your blood-a blot on your escutcheon- a rent in your garment-a death's head at your banquet.
There we have it. Sir, in order that my references to the position of the maritimes may be better understood I must refer back briefly to the history of confederation and the condition of the relations between the maritimes and the Dominion of Canada over the years. Only in that way can we hope to identify and correct the causes of the present condition.
In 1867 the maritimes had a fairly mature economy. They were growing rapidly. For example, for 10 years before confederation the colony of Nova Scotia was growing at a much more rapid rate than that of lower Canada. They prospered in an economy that had for its mainstays wood, wind and water. It was the day of sail, and the maritimes had become an important trading area in the

The Budget-Mr. MacLean world. They built wooden ships with which they traded to all parts of the world. They found themselves in a fairly booming economy. For example, at that time the city of Saint John was the fourth city in British North America. The colonies had negotiated trade agreements with the United States which were very beneficial to them. At that time New Brunswick was manufacturing 7-8 per cent of the Canadian production. The percentage has now dropped to 1-6.
When representatives of those colonies met in Charlottetown in 1864 their original idea was that they could become even more prosperous if the four Atlantic provinces united. This idea met with the favour of the then colonial secretary, who was the Duke of Newcastle. But owing to political reasons, Upper and Lower Canada found themselves in a political stalemate; and because of fear of the United States they sponsored and in the end had accepted the larger union.
The maritimes did not at any time receive this idea of a larger union with any great enthusiasm. The only colony that put it to the test of a popular vote was the Tilley government in New Brunswick, and they were soundly thrashed the first time they went to the people on the question of confederation. It was only at a later election when many other factors were involved which, according to some, muddied the waters, that a government in favour of the larger confederation was elected. After all, it may be only coincidental that the 1860's were the closing years of the golden age of the maritimes. It was an age when shipping was changing over from wooden ships and sail to steam and steel.
People will say that confederation was only coincidental with that, and there is no connection between the two. Nevertheless it would seem to me that since the maritimes had made such a success of things in the first field, they might have been able to compete successfully in the second as well under similar conditions.
Of course there were other reasons why confederation at that time was not especially popular. There was no great desire in the maritimes for union with the Canadas. There was little trade between them and almost no traffic. A Halifax paper of the day said:
We do not know each other. We are shut oS from each other geographically, commercially, politically and socially. Our interests are not identical but the very opposite.
As a matter of fact the colonies had almost nothing in common. When confederation took place the maritime provinces found themselves forced into an unnatural trade position.

The maritime economy had depended on shipping and trading north and south along the Atlantic seaboard. They found themselves forced into trading relations of an unnatural kind across barriers between themselves and the other colonies following confederation. They found, too, that as time went by their voice in the affairs of the new nation grew less and less. When the maritimes joined confederation they had a representation of 34 members out of 181 in this chamber. That representation has fallen to 26 members out of 265 at the present time. That gives one a clue to the lessening importance of the maritime provinces in Canada.
As I said before, these various colonies were something of the same order in size when confederation took place. At that time the maritimes had an area of about 50,000 square miles. Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba together had about six times that area, but it was not considered that the sizes were completely disproportionate as the maritimes was a more highly developed area with a denser population. We find today that the maritimes have the same area they had at confederation, whereas the other three provinces among them have increased their area by 738,000 square miles, bringing their total area at the present time to over one million square miles.
The extra area these provinces have added since confederation is one and a half times as great as the total area in Europe overrun by Russia since 1939. This, of course, is not a fair comparison, because the additional area was practically uninhabited when it was allotted to these provinces; however, its natural wealth is very great. It is the riches of these northern areas that are now keeping the cash registers of the industrial centres of Ontario and Quebec ringing.
It is not accidental that this state of affairs has come about. Upper and Lower Canada had scarcely entered confederation when they started a campaign to increase their boundaries until eventually they reached the size to which I have already referred. The tragedy of the matter is that the men of the day did not appear to realize what was taking place. No long or thoughtful debates took place on the subject when it came before this chamber at various times in 1908 and 1911.
In 1908 a resolution was passed approving of the entire area stretching north to Hudson bay being appended to the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba. The act was actually passed in 1911. It is true that hon. members from the maritimes raised their voices in protest at that time. They pointed out that this would upset the unit of representation. It being at the time the population of Quebec divided by 65, since the area of

Quebec was to be increased that would make the unit of representation greater and thereby decrease the representation of the maritimes and other areas in this parliament. Very few people, however, appeared to recognize the true significance of what took place.
In reading over the debate I did notice that one man apparently recognized exactly what was taking place and forecast fairly accurately what would occur. I am pleased that this man happened to be a resident of my riding, who very capably represented in this house for many years the riding which I now have the honour to represent. This gentleman's name was Alexander Martin and on that occasion he said:
The province of Quebec at present is the size of a pretty large kingdom. Some years ago more than half its original area was added to that province, and by this proposal another kingdom in extent is to be given it. To whom do these lands belong that we so cheerfully give away? What right has this government or any government to alienate the property of Canada and give it to any province without a consideration in return?
Then he went on to say:
... I protest strongly against the public domain being given away to the other provinces without some quid pro quo to the maritime provinces which cannot have their areas extended. Look at the preponderating influence over the smaller provinces which this extension of area will give to the larger provinces in this parliament.
And finally he said this:
The Prime Minister told us that this territory would not be settled for years to come, but we do not know the value of these lands. There may be millions and millions of acres of mineral lands worth incalculable wealth there. Before the house proceeds in this we should know exactly what we are giving away and how much of the wealth of the country we are divesting ourselves of.
That is the situation with regard to this matter.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was the date of that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it was July 13, 1908, and it is reported in column 12798 of Hansard.
Our object in the maritimes is to make confederation work if at all possible. We have been long suffering in the economic field. We have taken the attitude that we should turn the other cheek. As a matter of fact, by this time we have turned all four of them and we have been either slapped or kicked according to what seemed to be most appropriate at the moment.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to create the impression that maritimers think the larger provinces are not scrupulously fair. Most maritimers take the attitude that the larger provinces and the dominion as such believe in the principle of share and share alike. The only catch is that when the shares are being d^alt out, maritimers feel the assets go to
The Budget-Mr. MacLean the larger provinces and the liabilities go to the maritimes. There has been no adequate restitution to the maritime provinces for these vast kingdoms that were rather blithely given to these three provinces in particular. It is true that commissions have been set up to deal with this problem, and the Duncan and White commissions did deal with it and arrived at a formula which for that day was quite fair. However, due to inflation and other considerations, the reports made by those commissions are now out of date and no longer deal with the situation.
I have dealt with the position of the maritimes as compared with the other provinces, and later I hope to deal with the position of the maritimes, as well as other provinces, in relation to the central government, the unfavourable position of the maritimes, especially in the field of taxation, as compared with the position of the central government. The maritimes find themselves the victims of both conditions and therefore are struggling along under a double load of injustice.
At the time of confederation certain demands were made by the provinces before they would agree to come into confederation. The central government took over provincial debts and where the per capita debt was low agreed to pay 5 per cent interest on the difference between such low debt and the average per capita debt. There was to be a subsidy of 80 cents per head paid each year, which still exists. Before certain fields of taxation were handed over by the colonies to the federal government there was an understanding that since they were handing over rights to impose tariff duties and other indirect taxes, they should receive certain benefits in return. Those benefits were calculated at that time, but now they seem to be looked upon by the central government as handouts to the various provinces rather than rights which were turned over by the provinces to the central government as one of the conditions of coming into confederation.
At the time of confederation the taxation fields were divided between the provincial and federal governments, but it turned out that the field given to the federal government developed into a more lucrative one than that which was retained by the provinces. Because of this in many cases the provinces find themselves in a condition of penury which reduces them to a sort of vassalage to the central government, a condition which was never intended to exist, which it was never intended by the fathers of confederation should ever be created. In this connection I should like to quote briefly from speeches made in the past in this chamber by various

The Budget-Mr. MacLean ministers. On March 25, 1907, Sir Wilfrid Laurier had this to say:
Lower Canada would not have entered confederation if, as a consequence, she had been obliged to resort to direct taxation to levy the revenues necessary to carry on her domestic affairs. What was true of Lower Canada was equally true of the maritime provinces. Nova Scotia. New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, would not have agreed to enter confederation if, as a consequence, direct taxation had to be resorted to . . . Therefore it is not to be wondered at that when the provinces represented at that conference agreed to surrender to the central government the exclusive power of taxation by way of customs and excise, they should at the same time have stipulated as a condition precedent that a certain portion of the revenue thus collected should be returned to them, and a portion sufficient to permit them, without having recourse to direct taxation, to carry on their provincial affairs.
That was the principle under which the provinces joined confederation. Another situation has grown up which makes the financial position of the provincial governments extremely difficult. I refer to the system of matching grants which the central government seems to consider as something in the form of a gift. At times the central government will suggest a program which entails matching grants, but it is quite obvious that what may look like equality is not equality. These matching grants should be based on some ratio which has a relationship to the taxing facilities of the province concerned as compared with those of the federal government. Many provinces find that they would like to carry on some of these programs, but their position is like the position I would be in if the Aga Khan offered to pay one-half of the cost of certain fancy things which I could not afford. It is quite obvious which one of us would go broke first. In other words, something that we cannot afford is not a bargain. I am glad to see that there has been some correction of this sort of thing with regard to the trans-Canada highway, but that does not go far enough.
There is an urgent need for action to meet the position in which the provinces, especially the maritime provinces, find themselves. There should be a revision of the grants paid to the maritimes in lieu of public lands. There should be an attempt to correct the position where there is a great difference in the size and importance of the provinces. Possibly we could contemplate the creation of a couple of new provinces in the vast areas of northern Ontario and Quebec, provided the residents of those areas were agreeable. I know that in northern Ontario there is an association working to that end, and in that connection I should like to quote briefly from a speech made in this house by Sir

Wilfrid Laurier on July 13, 1908, with regard to that very thing, when he said:
If the territory of Ungava, which includes 456,000 square miles, were of the same character as to soil and climate as the valley of the St. Lawrence, we would not ask to have it added to the province of Quebec, but would make it another province. The conditions, however, are such that it is not possible to expect any large influx of population into that country. In fact, we cannot expect any influx of population there at all unless there should be the discovery of very large mineral deposits.
These large mineral deposits have been discovered and have sustained a great influx of population. I feel confident that if Sir Wilfrid Laurier were looking over the situation today and it were as it existed in 1908, a separate province probably would have been created.
I think it is important that there should be a careful study of the possibility of a complete reallotment of taxing powers between the provinces on the one hand and the central government on the other, in line with the spirit of confederation. In line too with the spirit of confederation, consideration should be given to the fiscal needs of the provinces, and any subsidies given to them should have relation thereto. In this connection I should like to quote briefly from Mr. J. A. Mathieson who, as a member of the White commission dealing with this matter during the 1930's, wrote a memorandum of dissent in the report of the commission:
I may shortly state my opinion on the result, which is:	That vital questions referred to this
commission remain undetermined by this report, and that the increase of subsidy proposed will give but partial and temporary relief. The lapse of more than eight years since the Duncan report went into effect granting provisional subsidies only, has witnessed such necessary increase in government expenditures in the case of all the provinces as will quickly absorb the present proposed increases, and still leave them in a position to compel diminution of necessary expenditure on provincial services, or a further increase of provincial debt or of local taxation, or of all three combined.
That is exactly what has happened.
These old British colonies that formed the Atlantic bulwark of British North America, after bearing their full share of the cost of Canadian organization and development, should not be treated with less justice and consideration than is being accorded the provinces whose lands they helped to purchase, to protect and equip for settlement.
The evidence produced before this commission showed from early days a total absence of equality in the treatment of the different provinces in Canada, both in regard to money grants by way of subsidy and in the gifts of vast areas of dominion lands to some provinces without any uniform plan and without any compensation to provinces that did not share in the partition of the common property.
It was made clearly to appear on this inquiry that one of the major problems facing Canada today is the devising of some general plan for the adjustment of dominion and provincial financial relations.

I suggest that that problem still faces us. In the province to which I belong, for example, in 1921 the provincial debt was $858,000; in 1926, at the time of the Duncan commission, it was $1,800,000; at the time of the White commission it had risen to $3,900,000; and since that time it has risen to $21 million. It has increased by about five times.
I would suggest, too, that beneficial legislation that has been approved by this house for various parts of Canada should be made applicable to the whole country, if at all possible. Legislation coming under that category, of course, is the P.F.R.A. and other similar legislation. There should be a restoration of the effective maritime freight rates, the benefits of which have been reduced seriously by the manner of applying horizontal freight rate increases over the post-war years. There should be a decentralization of industry for economic, socialogical and defence reasons. It is true that there has been some relief in this direction, as for example the creation of the large military camp at Gagetown, certain public works in the maritimes and so on. But these things are palliatives; they are not cures. They do not get to the root of the trouble. There should be co-operation between the federal government and the provinces, where necessary, in the development of power sources, whether they be hydroelectric, atomic energy or other sources of power.
Recently a proposal was made at the interprovincial conference with regard to the necessity of reviewing the question of subsidies to the maritimes in lieu of northern land. It is not my intention to go into the details of this proposal made on behalf of the maritime provinces, except briefly to say that if the proposal were followed-and it appears to be a logical one-there would be a very considerable increase. The subsidy figures for New Brunswick under this scheme would be $7,200,000, as against $900,000 at the present time; for Nova Scotia $10,400,000 as compared with the present figure of $1,300,000; and for Prince Edward Island, $2,200,000 as against $273,000. The total additional cost of this proposal to the federal government would be only $17,327,000.
Owing to the limitation of time I have had to give a good deal of attention to the difficulties under which the maritimes labour, and that no doubt has created an unbalanced picture of the real facts. We in the maritimes, although we are conscious of these disadvantages, are also conscious of the possibility of a great future. In the economic field, there are new resources being discovered. New water power sources are being developed.
The Budget-Mr. Bourque There is a decrease in the differential between the cost of the production of hydroelectric power and that of power from other sources. As time goes on this will mean that our position relative to other parts of the country will improve. There is an increasing population in the country and in the world, which creates a larger market for our agricultural and fish products.
There is evidence of new interest on the part of maritimers themselves in improving their economic position. The Atlantic provinces economic council is an illustration of that. However, we in the maritimes realize that perhaps the greatest values in this world are intangible and that economic progress is only a prerequisite to real living and should not be an end in itself. We place great value on the privilege of living in the maritimes. We place great value on the type of society we have there. We place great value on higher education, which has been a tradition in the maritimes. We have a pride in our homeland and a pride in our traditions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I add my congratulations to the Minister of Finance on his able presentation of the annual budget, one of the most important state documents of the year. The minister has proved to be a worthy successor to a long line of distinguished Canadians who have occupied this high post and who have presented to this chamber this annual summary of Canadian finances.
The Canadian budget is a document of vital importance to every citizen, to every business in this country and to every type of organization and association. Many people wait anxiously each year for the disclosure of the government's financial policies and decisions because their personal or business budgets in turn are affected by the tax and spending programs announced here in Ottawa.
It is important, then, that the Canadian budget be realistic, that it be practical and that it be so designed as not to upset or interfere with business expansion but rather contribute to it. The minister in his budget this year has taken into consideration the economic facts which lie behind this period of unprecedented prosperity, as well as the financial needs of government and probable developments in the future.
To the anxious taxpayer who constantly seeks reduction in taxation together with
2876	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Bourque increased public services, the 1956 budget may appear to be disappointing. It may also be disappointing to those political commentators and sensational news writers who constantly seek to provide their readers or listeners with controversial items. There is nothing controversial about the 1956 budget. It is a sound businessman's budget based on sound economic principles and shaped in accordance with economic facts. The minister has not introduced change for the sake of change or to make political capital. He has left business and individuals undisturbed except in those very few instances where new action or modification was essential. That is the basis of good budget making, and we on this side of the house are proud that it is the work of one of our most distinguished colleagues.
The sound and continuing policy of this government, stated many times by the Prime Minister, is exemplified in the new budget. The Prime Minister has continually sought to give the kind of leadership to this country that would result in a greater measure of prosperity for all our people, and that would combine with that prosperity an ever-increasing measure of security. The results of this national policy are plain to see. Canada has never enjoyed such prosperity. No , other country in the world is experiencing such a period of economic and social advancement. Canada today is the envy of nations. It has the most promising future. It is constantly attracting the capital and the manpower from other older and once richer countries because it has become the recognized land of opportunity.
Industry flourishes in lands where the government is stable, where taxation and government spending are realistic and based on actual needs, where there is no untidy experimenting with fiscal policies in a search for unattainable Utopias. This is not an experimental government; neither is it. an overcautious government. Over the years its policies, many of them reflected in the annual budgets, have been such as to encourage industrial and scientific development, the expansion of our towns and cities, more efficient agriculture and more and happier leisure time for our people. All those are the legitimate and wholesome aims of good government, and all those are reflected in this year's budget.
To those corporations and individuals who express disappointment because the budget does not contain substantial or important tax reductions, there is one very simple and logical answer.

Immigrants from other countries have come to Canada since the war and have achieved outstanding success. There are countless incidents which I could cite here today. Small businesses have been started by new Canadians with very limited capital and have soon expanded beyond the wildest dreams of their founders. Heads of families have come here and secured employment, and in an extremely short space of time have been able to bring out their families and provide them with what many of them considered to be luxurious housing and all the comforts of life. Just a few days ago I was told of a young woman from Great Britain who came here just six months ago, secured employment as a stenographer, and now with her savings is planning a holiday in her home country. She can scarcely believe that it is true. The heavy tax burden which we hear so much about has not injured her nor many others who have come here to live.

The financial policies of this government exemplified by the budget, should serve as a guide to business management and to individuals concerned about their own economic future.
Canada's prosperity is not an economic accident which a political party anxious for power can seize and exploit. It is something which, carefully tended and intelligently employed, can last for many years, increasing each year and adding more to our abundant life.
