subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before the six o'clock adjournment, the minister in his budget has taken into account the growing importance of the creative arts in Canada and has offered encouragement to those who seek to portray this country through artistic and editorial media. A high standard of living is of supreme importance but recognition must also be given to the fact that there is more to life than the science of economics. Over the years this government has given support and encouragement to the national gallery, which will soon be housed in its new building. In the budget it takes a further step by making available to Canadian art students freer access to the great masters. The admission of works of art to this country is to be encouraged, and the cultural heritage of the country is to be enriched.
In the same way the government seeks to assist and encourage those who endeavour to give Canadians a picture of their own country, by encouraging the writing and illustrative arts through the publication of Canadian magazines. Good Canadian publications expressing Canadian ideas and devoted to Canadian subjects are essential. Yet because of our small population the circulation of such magazines is necessarily limited. Next door, in the United States, we have the vast circulation magazines whose publishers look upon Canada as a bonus market, an overflow area where extra profits are to be picked up at small cost.
The Budget-Mr. Bourque
Some of these American publishers have moved into this country and print their magazines, sometimes here from American plates and sometimes in the United States, with a maple leaf on the cover and call them Canadian editions. Their editorial and illustrative costs are already covered by their home circulation. They are able to produce these Canadian editions at a fraction of the cost which competing Canadian publishers must pay for their productions. They pay nothing here to writers or illustrators, to our printing house compositors or engravers; they use their own presses and save money on freight and postage.
This is not fair competition, but if it were only economically unfair, we might be content to leave the matter there. It is ideologically unfair because American ideas, some of which may be in conflict with Canadian thinking, are circulated widely with the support of Canadian advertisers whose business has been weaned away from the Canadian publishers. The publisher of one of these quasi-Canadian editions has protested that this new tax imposed on these publications is discriminatory, unfair and not in the public interest. In his own defence he points out that his magazines are printed in this country and thus provide employment for Canadian labour. In reply I might point out to him that the principal thing in his magazines that is not Canadian is the editorial content. In other words the ideas are foreign, masquerading as Canadian.
No one objects to the importation of American publications which are just what they say they are. People who prefer to read them may do so, knowing that what they read is of foreign origin. But those publications which portray themselves as Canadian editions, solicit Canadian advertising and then spread foreign ideas should legitimately be taxed. I have no hesitation in agreeing that this is discriminatory; most Canadians, I believe, would wish it to be so. We wish to discriminate in favour of our own people, in favour of our own artists, our own writers, and in favour of our own ideology. That much-discussed item in the minister's budget deserves our full support.
While no one in Canada would wish to quarrel with the United States or prevent their ideas and opinions from being heard in this country, we all recognize the need for established media through which the Canadian viewpoint can be expressed, and this expression must be allowed to compete with American ideas on a fairer basis in this country. We believe in the sincerity of American ideas but we also wish to express our own ideas freely and forcefully. I don't
2878	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Bourque believe any United States citizen would quarrel with our right to maintain in this way our Canadianism.
We are entering a period in Canadian history when able and intelligent leadership in economic, cultural and ideological matters is of the utmost importance. Ahead of us lies the new industrial revolution implied by the term "automation". The science of electronics promises to alter many of our present methods of production and promises also to create new problems for us on the industrial front.
Management in this country is facing a period of keen competition and sweeping changes in practices. In many large industries today the volume of activity is too great for existing capabilities. Industry must do some intensive planning for the years immediately ahead.
We must in the near future draw a parallel between the services of geologists and physicists in the development of our raw resources over the past quarter century and the skilled technical services which are required today. We in government and we in business must take the scientific approach to our new problems. We will have at our disposal electronic devices which will perform functions in forecasting, statistical recording and data processing. These are all practical aids to clear business thinking, if they are properly used.
It is not sufficient for this government to content itself with providing experts in many professions. Industry, too, must take positive steps to provide itself with experts in a great many fields if it is to be able to cope with the problems in our new industrial world. Automation must not be just an industrial gadget; it must, without injuring business and without upsetting our economic system, serve producers and consumers alike. We cannot permit automation to become a Frankenstein that will destroy all that we have created.
There will be fields for vast new investments, greater than any we have heard of in the past. Industry here must keep pace with that in other lands, yet it must proceed with intelligent caution. Overproduction made possible by automation may increase unemployment and thus reduce still further the consumer market for the products overproduced. New capital investments on a large scale may injure beyond repair industries now in operation.
While these may seem to be problems of industry alone, they are problems affecting the whole business of government. They are 

viewed with concern by our responsible ministers, and they are incorporated in the economic thinking behind the budget which is now before this house.
In Canada we are extremely fortunate in having a great many intelligent, patriotic businessmen who in numerous ways serve the interests of their country. To be successful in business or in a profession has never been labelled a crime in this country, and I hope it never will be. Nor has it ever been considered anything but desirable that men who have made a success in their calling should devote some of their time and talents to public service. Far too often we hear people suggest that politics is a dirty business. It will be a dirty business if we do everything in our power to prevent decent citizens from taking part in politics. That should surely not be the wish of any individual or group in this house.
It was therefore with surprise and disappointment that I listened to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam make a serious personal attack upon a gentleman known to many of us as an honourable man, a successful corporation lawyer, a man of good reputation who has consented to accept an office in a political party because he believes it is his duty to give some of this time to public affairs. I refer to Mr. Duncan Kenneth MacTavish.
Mr. MacTavish holds many responsible positions. We talk of the lack of opportunity for Canadians in this country and the need for bringing in foreigners with brains and know-how, yet Mr. MacTavish by his own career serves as an inspiration to many of our youth. He believes in this country and he believes that as a private citizen he has a right and an obligation to participate in its political activities. As such he has been honoured by the Liberal federation, which elected him chairman. I suppose that any other political group paying similar honour to one of its followers would think it was a privilege to do so, and I would agree that is true. It is certainly not a reason for slander.
This government welcomes an interest by all men and women of good will in public affairs. We greet those who devote serious attention to politics which, after all, is only the science of government. And we are happy as supporters of the present government to direct their attention to the present budget, which we believe incorporates all the features of sound business administration and good common sense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I shall not be quite so lavish with my compliments in the direction of the Minister of Finance as the speaker

who has just taken his seat. However, we shall devote some few minutes to some of the problems we think are worth bringing before this house. First, just to set the minds of the government at ease, I must tell them that we are going to vote in favour of the amendment, the first line of which reads:
This house regrets that the budget is empty.
I am sorry to say we find that the amendment is also a little bit empty. However, we are going to vote non-confidence in the government on account of their failure to implement fiscal and financial policies which we believe are necessary in the good administration of Canadian business.
There is one other thing that has worried me quite consistently, and that is to find just where Her Majesty's loyal opposition stands on certain principles which we hear quite a lot about. We hear them continuously recommending tax cuts and relief for those in the lower income brackets. Of course that is more pronounced this session than formerly, and I would just like to put a paragraph on the record again because I believe it contains some very fine words. It is found on page 2550 of Hansard, and is taken from the address given by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell):
I fear I have not been as forceful as I would have liked in speaking for the hundreds of thousands of our fellow citizens who have been and continue to be. in so far as this government is concerned, forgotten men and women. I only wish that I could din my words into the ears of every serious, every generous, every responsible citizen of this country and that I might have the gift to persuade them that it is their duty to rise up and demand action.
I would just like to tell the hon. member for Greenwood I am afraid his words were not very well received by members of his own group, especially when we recall that just a couple of nights ago they voted against an amendment which condemned this government for not bringing tax relief to those in the low income bracket.
Let me come to the budget. We have heard it called by various names, and have read various articles dealing with it, but the one that appealed to me most was a heading in the Ottawa Journal, as follows: "Harris Comes With Little". To my mind this is about the most concise summing up of the budget that could have been given; and the little that is in the budget also makes it that much harder for us to find something to talk about.
Very little information was given to us that had not been available in the press and through other channels before the night of the budget speech, but again I am thinking possibly that is the policy of this government. Throughout this session and the two
The Budget-Mr. McLeod previous sessions that I have had the privilege to sit in the house, I have come to the conclusion that this government has developed to a high degree the art of withholding information from parliament, and comes up with little when questions are asked. At this stage I should like to mention the fact that you can take the order paper of today and you will find simple questions standing there for two months that still remain unanswered. Many times when the answers are given they are not just quite as full of information as we think they should be.
However, in this budget there was one thing I noticed on which I should like to comment, namely the fact that the sales and excise tax structure of this country will be referred to a commission with the idea of finding out the best level at which those taxes should be levied and collected. I brought this matter before the house a year ago in connection with car dealers. I feel that levying those taxes at the level of the manufacturer is discriminatory against those dealers.
I am glad to know that this is to be a subject for study; but I understand, again from the press, that the level that will be recommended is the wholesale level. I do not believe that is the proper level at which to levy this tax. I think the tax should be levied at the retail level. It will bring to the attention of the people the huge costs they are facing daily in the operation of this government, and it will also be quite a lot fairer, in that the tax is paid immediately by the party on whom it was intended to be levied, and it will be the actual tax that will reach the government.
Under the present system, because the tax is levied at the manufacturer's level, it is pyramided up by the price spreads until, when it reaches the consumer, in spite of being a tax of 8 per cent to 10 per cent, it is possibly increased from 75 per cent to 100 per cent. Therefore I am satisfied that if this tax were collected at the retail level the government could cut the tax by perhaps 50 per cent and realize the same amount of money, and the price of the goods to the consumer would be reduced accordingly.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat spoke very strongly in favour of the tax on advertising in the so-called Canadian issues of United States magazines. I must add my voice to those which strongly oppose this tax. I maintain that these companies which publish magazines in Canada are not different from branches of United States companies doing business here in the ordinary way, if I may express it in those terms. I am sure that if we were to levy any discriminatory tax against the products of such
2880	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. McLeod companies we would certainly be in a bad way. It is not only the ordinary fair-minded people of Canada who look upon this tax as being discriminatory; many publishers are also opposed to it. I think I would be safe in saying that most publishers hold this view. I trust that the minister will give this further consideration and will bow to the storm of disapproval that is rising from coast to coast.
There is one other subject in the budget, Mr. Speaker, which I believe has not been mentioned thus far by any speaker; I know that the minister made no reference to it. I am referring to the alarming increase in the national debt of this country and the cost of servicing this debt. I like to compare the government and its affairs to a large business organization, and truly it is the largest business enterprise in Canada. I am satisfied that the government, which I choose to liken to the board of directors of an industrial concern, and the Minister of Finance, who might be likened to its manager, would face serious questioning by the shareholders of the company if year after year the annual report presented to them showed increased debt, increased overhead and an increased cost for interest.
We find that for the year 1956-57 interest on our national debt is going to amount to over $500 million. I recently took a few minutes in which to figure this out, and I discovered that for every second the clock ticks during the next 12 months we are going to pay out money to the cost of servicing our national debt at the rate of $16.03; every second for 12 full months, day and night without let up.
We must take stock of that large amount of money and perhaps think in terms of welfare, our old age pensioners, our blind and disabled. Perhaps we should think of it in terms of hospital insurance, which I am glad to note will possibly be introduced in Canada. Whenever we in the opposition ask for increased grants for these worthwhile causes we are told quite plainly that the government does not have the money or we are met with the question, "Where will the money come from?"
Mr. Speaker, over $500 million is being spent needlessly in interest charges. We who have been frequently looked upon as crazy-money people and who have been described in similar terms advocate a system for creating debt-free money for the service of this country. We do not think this can be brought into effect overnight, but it can be brought about gradually as our bonds are retired and the obligations taken up. We maintain it is the right of this government to honour them. When that is done, new debts could be


financed with debt-free money and eventually we would eliminate the needless spending of this sum amounting to over $500 million. This money could be used for welfare purposes. Just think how happy the Minister of Health and Welfare would be if he had that amount of money to put into welfare plans for the benefit of the people of Canada. I sometimes wonder if those in our group are as crazy as is generally supposed.
As I said a moment ago I am pleased to note that a national plan of hospital insurance is being proposed. I have in my hand a Social Credit manifesto, a publication of which we are quite proud, and I would just like to read a section to you:
National Health Program
The most valuable resource in any nation is its citizens. The health of every individual citizen is therefore one of Canada's greatest national assets. The Social Credit Association of Canada believes that it is the constitutional responsibility of the Canadian government to provide the provinces with unconditional per capita grants for the following purposes:
1. To enable the provinces to establish an adequate system of health services accessible to all.
We in this group believe that the proper way to institute a service of this kind is under provincial administration. Although the proposed system of the federal government does not quite follow along those lines, I am greatly impressed by the tremendous spirit of co-operation which the Minister of National Health and Welfare assures us will be made evident in bringing this plan into effect. As I have said on other occasions, I believe that the less government we have at the top, the better things will be; and the closer we can bring the administration of welfare to the people themselves, the more effective it will be.
The plan proposed by the federal government is a step in the right direction, but it is only a step and it is not perfect. We know it will be enlarged, and we know that nothing begins in a state of perfection. As long as the department continues to show the spirit of co-operation which is being manifested at the present time I am satisfied that many of the difficulties that arise in the minds of the people will be overcome.
Perhaps one of the greatest reasons for opposition to the proposed scheme is that it does not cover tuberculosis and mental illness. I realize that this is only a start and we cannot look for perfection, but these are two forms of illness that are being pretty well taken care of in Canada today. It is true that a large part of the expense is being borne by the provinces. I must admit, and I do so gladly, that a large part of the funds for tuberculosis and mental illness control

and research comes from the federal department of health. The institutions to which victims of these diseases are committed will not become a part of our national health scheme. All cases of tuberculosis and mental illness that can be handled in the wards of our general hospitals will be covered by this plan. So it is not as bad as some people would think.
Since we are dealing with mental illness I think it might be wise to spend a couple of minutes more on this important subject. We hear about heart disease being a great killer; we hear about the terrible ravages of arthritis; we hear of the dread and dire effects of cancer. There is no one who is more aware than I of the dangers and terrors of these diseases, but when we stop to think that 50 per cent of the patients in Canada are mental patients then I think it is time we gave a few minutes to considering this great problem.
It is not only the patient himself who must suffer; there is the trouble and worry to the immediate family. It is true that today mental illness carries no stigma, that it is considered to be nothing more than an illness of a part of the body the same as any other; nevertheless there are broken homes, there is worry and heartsickness much more than would meet the naked eye.
As I said, I should like to pay a tribute to the department for what has been done in connection with mental illness. We are not ready for any great curative program because this is something we know very little about. We would really get the greatest benefits from every dollar spent if it were spent on research. It is quite easy to get up and say that we should spend more money on research, but there is no use making money available unless we have the trained personnel and the trained professional men and women who can make use of that money.
In this respect the government is doing quite a noble work. Under its mental health program it has made available large sums of money. This program was set up in 1948-49, when $4 million was made available for mental health work. A total of $1,142,318 was allocated in that year, but the facilities available were able to make use of only the small sum of $439,128. This has grown year by year, until last year there was made available for mental health $7,177,855. The amount allocated was $6,635,947, and of that total allotment there was used under the supervision of the provincial departments of health a total of $6,013,547.
In a sense we are able to see a marked improvement in the facilities available to carry on research and the psychiatric treatment and care which is necessary in fighting this
The Budget-Mr. McLeod dread disease, this great striker-down of the health of the people. However, it will be noticed that although $7,177,855 was made available, all that could be used was a little over $6,000,000. So we are not ready yet. We can holler for more money, but there is no use providing more money until we have the facilities and the trained personnel to use it wisely.
But there is a program under way to train the required personnel. In the period 19481955 this resulted in the training of 229 psychiatrists, 129 psychologists, 190 psychiatric social workers, 183 psychiatric nurses and 6 occupational therapists, a grand total of 1,283 trained personnel. That is what has been accomplished under the training program during the past seven years.
But we still have a long way to go. It is felt that at the present time this country requires 498 psychiatrists, and we have just 326. There is room in the established institutions for that many at the present time. A total of 189 psychologists could be used, and we have only 111. We need 290 social workers and there are only 195 available. We need 358 occupational therapists and there are only 107. Occupational therapists are needed not only in connection with mental illness but in the general care of children and for cerebral palsy cases. In the case of administrative nurses we require 214 and we have only 175. We require 118 teaching nurses and we have only 66.
I would commend to this house a very wide program of teaching and training in order to make use of the money and resources available through our present department of health. Rather than holding out for grants to take care of people in institutions I figure, and I am sincere in this, that we can spend our dollars to much better advantage in research and study in order to prevent this type of illness. As I said, the provincial governments with the aid of the federal government have the facilities and are doing a good job.
There are a couple of what I might call local problems which I should like to bring to the attention of the house. The riding which I represent is pretty well in the centre of the interior of British Columbia. As I have said before, it is one of the finest dairying districts in British Columbia. In that small area we have about 15,000 dairy cows. It is estimated that our farmers have over $2 million invested in herds and breeding stock, and over $4,500,000 in farms and equipment.
Like every other industry, the dairy industry today is facing serious problems because of rising costs of production, and some
2882	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. McLeod assistance should be given to our farmers so they may be able to produce better pasture and provide better housing for their dairy herds. The old fashioned stall and stanchion is giving way to loose housing, but whether that will be the type of housing best adapted to our rather rigorous climate up in the north Okanagan remains to be seen. Some experimental work should be done along these lines. Then there is the matter of producing feed. Our acreage is limited and we must produce the greatest number of tons it is possible to produce on every acre of our land.
The matter of disease is becoming quite serious in these herds, though they are not different from herds in other parts of Canada. Mastitis, brucellosis, vibrio fetus, milk fever, bloat; these are all of great worry to our dairy farmers. We are far removed from any pathological centre where treatment or diagnosis are available. I was talking to a dairyman just before I came east, and he told me that this vibrio fetus is a disease that is becoming quite prevalent and quite serious. Of course the immature calf which has been dropped dead has to be sent away for diagnosis. We have no facilities in the interior, and the only place where this can be done is at the university in Vancouver. By the time you get one of the samples sent away and it reaches the dissection tables at the laboratory of the University of British Columbia it is in such a state of decay that it is impossible to make a correct diagnosis.
So I would like to bring to the attention of this house the need for experimental farm services in northern Okanagan. We are not going so far as to ask for what might be called a complete experimental farm. At the present time at Summerland, a little over 100 miles to the south of us, in mainly fruit producing country, we have an experimental farm where, mostly as a sideline, a dairy herd is maintained. We believe that the proper place to have that dairy herd housed is in the North Okanagan or Shuswap area. I am sure some arrangement could be made without too great expense, perhaps on a co-operative basis with one of our leading dairymen in that area, whereby this herd could be housed and experiments could be carried on in cooperation with an official from the farm at Summerland. The whole institution could be carried on as a substation under Summerland jurisdiction.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not have something to say about the P.F.R.A. Last fall the Minister of Agriculture, when he was in Vernon, touched on this and told


us, "We cannot have the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act in British Columbia. You know, this was just set up to take care of the Palliser triangle and so on in the prairies, and there is no further provision." But I should think if there were any genuine desire on the part of the Minister of Agriculture to apply similar provisions to British Columbia there is nothing to stop such action being taken. I am sure we are not anxious to have the handle of "prairie farm" attached to us across the mountains, where we do not know much about the prairies. Possibly the name could be changed to the "national farm rehabilitation act", if the name "prairie" eliminates the use of that act in a province that does not happen to be a prairie province.
Recently I noticed that the irrigationists of British Columbia presented a brief to the Gordon commission. I am sure the government will have those figures, but I should like to place them on the record here tonight. In the Okanagan-Similkameen irrigation districts there are 36,526 acres under irrigation at the present time, and there is an additional potential of 21,584 acres. Private projects in this area have 6,812 acres watered, and 8,114 acres could be so watered. The Fraser-Thompson area has 72,000 acres under irrigation, with a potential of 110,000 acres.
I am sure the hon. members for Fraser Valley and New Westminster and our hon. friends from Burnaby-Coquitlam and Burnaby-Richmond, would be glad to see these regulations applied to that part of British Columbia, thus bringing an additional 100,000 acres under water. In the Columbia-Kootenay district there are 29,000 acres under irrigation and there is a potential of 60,000 acres. That gives us a total potential in the province of British Columbia that could be placed under water of 299,698 acres. This means that 9,849 farms of 20 acres could be taken out of that acreage. With a family of approximately five on each farm, it would give us land which could support a further population of approximately 50,000 people, who would not only be able to provide for their own living, but would be able to provide more of that food which is necessary to meet the requirements of the people of Canada and the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I came into the house a few moments ago in hopes that you would give me the privilege of the floor tonight, and I opened this bulky file, my young friend from Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) passed the remark that he hoped I was not going to read all this. Well, sir, I have not yet read a speech in this house, and I do not intend to begin tonight. My eyesight is not as good as

that of some hon. members who stand straight up and read every line of their speeches laid on the desk. I will admit that the style I use might not read so well in Hansard, but I assure you that it will be my own thoughts and the things I believe.
I hesitated to ask you for the privilege of speaking tonight and using the time of this house. Mr. R. B. Bennett, who knew something about figures, stated to my hon. friend the former member for Temiscouata, about 1931, that the cost of the sitting of parliament at that time was between $1,200 and $1,300 an hour, counting all the printing of Hansard, the notices and so on, the extra staff and everything else. Imagine what it would be today. Mr. Speaker, I must admit to you that in this session so far, although I have heard many fine speeches, I doubt that I have heard one that is worth $1,800 an hour.
But before I go any further I want to bring something to your attention, sir, which I think should have been raised as a question of privilege. My comments are those of a man who has sat in this assembly for many years, who for many years before sat in the legislative assembly of Alberta, whose direct ancestor on my mother's side was a member of the first assembly ever to sit in Canada under the Quebec Act. I wish to say that I have resented very much the accusation that has been made that we over here are just rubber stamps, that we are just followers.
In order to base my argument on the proper ground I should like to refer to the words of Montcalm, while still alive, to Brigadier Townshend, who commanded the English forces after the death of General Wolfe, with respect to what was understood at the time the so-called conquered race became.part of the British people. It is on record that Montcalm wrote:
Monsieur, the humanity of the English sets my mind at peace concerning the fate of the French prisoners, and the Canadians.
They were already a Canadian nation then. They understood him too.
Feel toward them as they have caused me to feel. Do not let them perceive that they have changed masters. Be their protector as I have been their father.
I believe, sir, those words of Montcalm should be placed on the records of this house because as a result of this attitude we have succeeded, through many years of struggle, in becoming a united and independent nation. We remember that some time ago the Minister of Agriculture made a speech at a convention. He said that he had read the speech of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1904 in which he expressed the thought that there would be as many people west of the 07509-183
The tsudget-Mr. Dechene great lakes by 1950 as there would be east of the great lakes. Unfortunately, with all his vision and his genius Sir Wilfrid could not know that there would be two terrible conflicts in the meantime which would change the course of events and prevent this great growth of the western provinces.
Under Laurier we had as minister of finance one of the best men, a man who led his province for many years as premier, W. S. Fielding. Later we had Robb, Dunning, Ralston, Ilsley. What a tremendous job Ilsley did during the war! Then we had Abbott and now we have the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). In spite of anything that had been said, and knowing the conditions under which the budget was brought down with, as every hon. member of the house knows, the danger of inflation, the Tory papers and the Tory politicians predicted exactly what the minister was going to do and once he did it they all criticized him bitterly because he had done so. I join his name with those of these other great ministers of finance. I do not hesitate to say that I am proud of him and we are all proud of him.

speechtext:
The greatest sport I know is to spend the other fellow's money. It does not cost you anything. You can stand up and say: Why do you not spend money on this, why do you not do that, why do you not increase family allowances, why do you not increase old age pensions, why do you not make a grant for this and a grant for that? It is so nice to be in the opposition and not have to raise the funds with which to do these things.
We have been accused of being irresponsible. I have given some of my record. I think I know what responsibility means as a public man. In 1953 I had an example of how irresponsible some people can be in order to win votes and elect one member. You remember the great promise made by the Leader of the Opposition that if he were elected he would reduce expenditures immediately by half a billion dollars. There was a gentleman in Athabaska, a friend of mine whom I will not name, who knew he could not be elected but thought he might try to rally whatever Tory forces were left in that corner of the world. A week later he came to see me. He had read the paper and he said to me, "The man who is going to reduce taxation and expenditure by half a billion dollars has just gone into Saskatchewan and said that if he is elected he will immediately construct the South Saskatchewan river dam, estimated to cost $350 million, in order to
2884	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Dechene elect one fellow in Saskatchewan." He said, "I am not going to run. I cannot understand that. How can you cut down expenditure by half a billion and the next day spend $350 million more? Even a school child in the seventh grade would not swallow that."
As I entered the house the other day I read the motto engraved in the granite on the west side of the peace tower, that motto which is so true, "Where there is no vision the people perish." Sir, I wish to present this thought. I wish to argue, to recommend, to demand that the great railway companies of this country keep their word to the people of the northern part of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, given at the time they entered into their agreements and received charters from this parliament. They promised to construct lines north of the Saskatchewan and Beaver rivers.
This may seem to be a local matter to most hon. members, but I say to you that there is a region 1,000 miles or more wide with unlimited possibilities. It is the gateway to the great northland through the Athabaska river. The region extends from Churchill through Prince Albert and my country into the Athabaska, Lac la Biche and the Peace river country. At Prince Albert you have the choice of two routes, one to the south leading to the great lakes and the new St. Lawrence seaway and the other one leading to Hudson bay and Churchill.
In Alberta in 1931 I seconded a motion to make Churchill a free port of entry. They thought I was a dreamer and that it was impossible. Yet if you look at the map for one moment you will realize the tremendous possibilities for the export of wheat, other cereals and cattle from western Canada through Churchill and there would be plenty of ships because they would come back loaded to a free port of entry and would be able to serve the prairies at cost. Today it comes by railroad and you have to pay through the nose, as it were, for this production. A free port of entry at Churchill would enable our farmers in the west to compete with the farmers in the east.
I was called a dreamer and visionary. I moved in this house and I moved in the house in Alberta that we should return the mineral rights to the owners of the soil. I got no support except from a few. Right at this moment, when everybody is up in arms, we are going back 45 years. It is reciprocity all over again; no truck or trade with the Yankees, the Yankees are going to conquer Canada, the Yankees are going to make us so rich that we will be unable to remain free. Forty-five years ago the same argument was used.

I took part in that election in 1911. If we had followed the suggestion I made, namely that the owners of the soil should be the owners of the mineral rights, there would have been a tremendous difference in the outcome of the administration of these vast mineral resources. In 66 per cent of the states those mineral resources belong to the owners of the soil. It did not stop the development, far from it. But it gave the settlers, the farmers, the local businessmen, a stake in this wealth so they got together and organized companies, and if there was a million dollars to be made it was not made by Imperial Oil but was made mostly by the people of the country, by the owners of the soil themselves.
I know it is too late now. Most of those resources have been alienated. But I am truly fed up with hearing about this fear of United States capital getting control of our country.
In 1923 I moved a motion. I speak about myself because I seem to be almost the only one left of the crowd of those days. I moved a motion in the Alberta house that in cooperation with the Canadian government we should offer help, give a prize of a considerable amount of money, to the first company, firm or individual which would bring in a 1,000-barrel oil well, and a $1,000 premium to the oil driller who drilled that well. We knew what happened in Calgary. We had discovered oil before anything you now have in Calgary. I hope the Calgary members are here. They have heard about the offer. Nobody took it up. If we listened to the opposition today we would wait forever until our Canadian friends, our real friends-I do not know where they are; they are certainly not in the Liberal party, or if they are they did not help me at election time-until these real men from Canada came along-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We should have to wait and today the oil would still be there; no development would have taken place.
Now I want to speak about those railroads. In 1909-that is a long time ago-the Liberal government in Alberta went into the railway construction business in this manner. We had a great wave of immigration under the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. People were pouring into the western plains, breaking the virgin bosom of the wealthy prairies and beginning this great production which is the marvel of today even in a nation

as rich and as well organized as the United States. But those people needed communication. They needed transportation. The Liberal government of the day made a deal or an offer, guaranteeing the debentures of the railway companies up to $15,000 a mile, in order to bring branch lines from Edmonton and Calgary into this country into which the settlers were pouring. The result was that from Edmonton straight north to Atha-baska 100 miles, from Edmonton to St. Paul, from Edmonton to my own town of Bonny-ville, from Edmonton to Fort McMurray in the riding of Athabaska, Alberta railways were built1 to the Peace river. These guarantees brought those lines to give transportation facilities to these settlers, farmers, and businessmen living there for their production. I wish we had a map large enough. There is your map represented by my extended arms, these lines all going out like the arms of an octopus, bringing trade to Edmonton. But every farmer in my country had to pay the backhaul of 175 or 200 miles into Edmonton and back again if he wanted to reach Winnipeg or the eastern market.
Mr. Speaker, I wish more time were available. I have not watched the clock very closely. I have here resolutions accepted unanimously by the assembly of Alberta with regard to the connecting of these lines to the Saskatchewan and Beaver rivers. This is not just a plan, as I said, it means an outlet and route for all this vast country north of Saskatoon and Prince Albert, north of the Saskatchewan river across the prairie, across the northern part of the province giving access to the Pacific ocean at Prince Rupert.
This is not a dream. Charters were issued. The C.P.R., knowing by that time the value of that north country, came to this parliament and demanded a charter. It was proposed and they received it. They were to build west of Prince Albert through Meadow Lake-this is built now, as those who come from that country know-to near Goodsoil, a place in northwestern Saskatchewan, where they meet the Canadian National Railways line from Battleford-St. Walburg into Cold Lake. According to the regulations laid down by this parliament the C.P.R. received running rights over 55 miles of the Canadian National Railways line from Goodsoil or nearby into Cold Lake in the constituency of Athabaska and began to build.
I have here the dates of the charters and everything. I know time does not allow me to refer to them, but the records are readily available. In 1931 the whole thing was stopped. I see that the Minister of Agriculture is in the house. One of his secretaries at that time was in charge of the removal of the 67509-183J
The Budget-Mr. Dechene settlers from the dry belt in southern Saskatchewan into the interior of northwestern Saskatchewan and northeastern Alberta which were to be served by these railroads and where we had rain, growth and grass, where we had everything. Literally thousands of people came from the south.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is people like you that prevented this country from going ahead. The hon. member is a defeatist or a poltroon, one of those who, after the first world war, began to agitate and to tell the people how unhappy they were, that our country was no good, that we were all broke. That agitator, a man who has meagre political capital, has used this policy of discouragement to achieve his own end. He is one of the men who prevented those railroads from being built. But today I am still pleading for those railroads to be built.
The same argument was used in a letter to my hon. friend from Vegreville a few months ago; a line north of the Saskatchewan river would serve part of his constituency. It was stated that it had not been proved to the satisfaction of the Canadian National Railways that the building of that gap of 39 miles from Bonnyville to St. Walburg and from Heinsburg to Frenchman Butte in Saskatchewan would produce enough revenue to warrant its construction. Well, why did they not use that argument when they built that part of the Canadian National in northern Ontario, where you can travel for a whole day without even seeing a rabbit? If the argument was good with respect to this gap, surely it would be worth something in northern Ontario.
About a month ago two ministers of the crown in Alberta went for a trip on the Canadian Pacific Railway to a place called Marwayne. This will be interesting to the Minister of Transport and to the Canadian National Railways. They told the people of Marwayne that a new bridge was going to be built over the Saskatchewan river at Lea Park, about 35 miles down the river from Elk Point, to provide another bridge between Edmonton and the boundary of Saskatchewan for the transport of agricultural products. And, sir, they stated that in one year over 10,000 head of cattle had crossed the river by ferry to go to the Canadian Pacific Railway south of the Saskatchewan river. That

The Budget-Mr. Dechene business was lost to the Canadian National Railways, and that is only one example. All the grain must cross the river, and so must other products.
There is a line in the province of Alberta that went about half way between the river and what they considered was the productive part of Alberta. Later on the Canadian Pacific Railway came along and obtained a charter to build from the Cut Knife and Lloydminster country, in between the C.N.R. and the river, to Edmonton. I think I would be safe in saying they took 70 per cent of the trade or business in that part of the country. The Canadian National Railways are watching the whole thing getting away from them while we are appealing to the government to have this gap closed. They say that the closing of this gap of 39 miles would not prove to be a paying proposition.
I hold in my hand three resolutions, but I shall not read them all. At the time they were presented I was a member of the opposition, and hon. members know how easy it is for a motion from the opposition to carry in the house. These resolutions are dated 1932, 1934 and 1935. In order to save time I shall read the shortest one, which is dated 1932:
Moved by Mr. Dechene, seconded by Mr. Falconer:
He was the provincial member for Atha-baska. He is still living.
That this assembly regrets the decision of the dominion government not to proceed with the construction of the extension of the Bonnyville-St. Walburg and the Heinsburg-Frenchman Butte lines of the Canadian National Railway lines from Edmonton to St. Walburg and Edmonton to Turtle-ford;
That under existing conditions the farmers of all that great district north and east of Edmonton have no direct access to eastern markets and are compelled to pay a back-haul on all the products shipped out and on merchandise imported into that district;
That a large number of settlers induced to settle in the districts to be served by the proposed lines will find themselves in a precarious position, and a large percentage of them, in need of relief;
That we respectfully urge the dominion government to reconsider the matter and to proceed with the construction of the said lines during the coming season.
The debate continued.
The motion being proposed Mr. Speaker declared the motion carried.
Nothing was done, and I am still here pleading for those settlers. I assure the ministers, the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific authorities, that I am seeking no political benefit out of this request presented on behalf of those farmers and those pioneers. In spite of that, they made good. With the courage of the western people, with the pioneering spirit of those


men and women, they made good in spite of the fact that they were so far away from the railroads. They came from the dry belt, with nothing whatever when they came there except old, worn-out horses and some wagons and a few head of cattle that were hardly able to walk, and in spite of the fact that they were this distance from transportation facilities they made good. But they still need those transportation facilities for which, sir, I have the privilege tonight to plead.
I may not long be able to speak on behalf of these people in this parliament of Canada. However, as long as God lends me life I intend to continue the work I began, because I was one of the men who went to Edmonton and then came to Ottawa in order to induce the railways run by the government to act on behalf of this great country to the north, east and west of Edmonton. There is an empire in the making there.
The other day a man who should know-let me mention his name; it was Mr. Sweezey from Montreal-wrote an article in the press in which he pointed out that the tremendous coal resources out west were not going to remain idle. He is one of the experts in this line. He said that with the immense quantity of coal we have in the west and in Alberta, power could be produced cheaper at those mines than could even be produced with white hydro, and he should know. The Calgary Power Company is building one of its largest units west of Edmonton, at Lake Wabamun. It will be completed shortly and will eventually develop some 350,000 horsepower right on top of a coal mine, because they know that the coal available is so extensive that it will last almost forever, and such a plant is so much cheaper to build and operate.
I should now like to speak about gas. When the natural gas question comes up I may have something further to say on it. When I come from home to Edmonton I drive through the Redwater oil field, and almost as far as you can look you can see the gas burning. They have to do it. When they hit the oil they pipe the gas away from it in another pipe, and they have to burn the gas to get rid of it. They have no way of using it. Well, they are doing that. They are burning the gas while we are talking about bringing it to the people of the east who need it.
When I was a young fellow 52 years ago,
I went down the Athabaska river. It was a great trip. Old Captain Shott was the captain. His name was Fosseneuve, but because he was the first man ever to shoot the rapids of the Athabaska they called him Captain Shott. The name remains even to this

day. His children and his grandchildren are called Shott. We went down the McMurray. It looked as if you were at the end of the world. I never thought I would reach there, but I did, and I am the representative of those people in this house tonight. I think of Fitzgerald, McMurray and Waterways. There you will find the greatest reserve of oil in the world. I refer to a report of the United States bureau of mines and of our own bureau of mines in Ottawa.
The officials will tell you that this is not a dream, nor is it a guess. They have found bituminous sands all over the country. They estimate that at least 500 billion-not million-barrels of oil will be available when they have found the way to separate the sand from the oil. It can be done. I said in this house some years ago that if these reserves had been in Germany at the time of the second world war they would have used the oil for their war machinery. All this potential is just 350 miles from Edmonton.
There is also there enough tar available to pave every road, street and lane in Canada. We continue to import tar from Trinidad and other places. Billions of tons of tar are available. Do you wonder at my asking for the floor tonight in order to bring this matter once again to the attention of the people of Canada and their elected representatives? This is the dream of my youth, the prosperity of this great land to the north and to the west with its vast possibilities. This is the great challenge to our young people.
I remember talking over the radio a short time ago in answer to an agitator, a demagogue who told us we could not do anything. I said we had heard that story back in 1920 after the first great war, and we heard it after the second world war. I say to them now that you do not have to look to the east, west, north or south; you merely have to look at what is staring you in the face in this wonderful land of ours with its incredible resources and indescribable wealth. This is indeed a challenge to our young men and women. I wish I were young so I could devote some more years of my life to bringing about the completion of the railway lines and help to develop Canada's resources for the welfare of the whole country. God in his wisdom knows best.
The other day I picked up a great newspaper, the Toronto Star Weekly. I found an article written by Harold Hilliard. The author writes from Skagway, Alaska, following a tour through the northern part
The Budget-Mr. Stanton of Alberta. I should like to quote one paragraph from this article:
The railroad proposal closest to reality is one which the federal government and the Canadian Pacific Railway have under active consideration. It involves a 350-mile extension of an existing line which terminates at Waterways, Alberta.
That is in the constituency of Athabaska.
It will be pushed north to the shores of Great Slave lake in the Northwest Territories. Here Consolidated Smelters of Trail, B.C., a Canadian Pacific Railway company, is reputed to have proven what may be the world's greatest deposit of lead and zinc.
The railway to develop Great Slave lake should be built from no other place but Fort McMurray-Waterways, because that is the end of the navigable water on this route. I hope there is some truth in the plan as outlined in this paper.
I hope I was not wrong in asking for the floor tonight; I know I am speaking under a handicap. Hudson bay to the Pacific, Port Arthur and Fort William to the Pacific; that is the country to develop, 1,000 miles of it. Millions are waiting for this through transportation line which should have been built long ago. We are surprised that Americans come here; perhaps they will build the line if we are unable to do it.
I should like to conclude my remarks with a thought I expressed on a previous occasion, and which now comes to mind again, sir. My thought refers to the incredible wealth and beauty of the land and the lakes which will soon be free from their shroud of ice and snow under the smiling sun of Alberta. The province is frequently referred to as sunny Alberta. When the beneficent being who attended to the work of all creation, who cast the stars, the comets and planets into limitless space and created all earth, and who then created men and women to inhabit it came to rest on the seventh day and cast a look upon his work and declared himself satisfied, I am sure that at that moment he had a glimpse of the beauties of the Athabasca and Peace river country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I shall try not to be repetitious in the few remarks I wish to make in regard to the disappointments of the budget, but I do wish to bring to the attention of the government certain problems that are plaguing the people of Canada, and more particularly the people of eastern Ontario.
The budget may be classed as something old and nothing new; something old because apparently the minister reached into last year's bag and drew out the same old 1955 budget; nothing new, for no doubt he is following the tactics of his predecessor, to>
The Budget-Mr. Stanton enable him to open the cupboard door and bring out a nice, large, juicy bone for next year's election.
The provinces of Canada are disappointed, the municipalities are disappointed and the people are disappointed. Now that the gross national product is increasing each year, and in all probability will show a substantial increase in 1956-indeed it has been estimated by the minister that the gross national product for the year 1956 will be $2 billion more than in 1955-surely the taxpayers are entitled to an easing of taxes, if a moderate amount of economy were practised.
I believe that if taxes were eased a certain amount it would stimulate production to such an extent that revenues would be even greater. A good illustration of this was the reduction of 5 per cent in the excise tax on automobiles last year. The minister forecast that the decrease would lower the revenue by $26 million; instead it increased sales to such an extent that the excise revenue increased by $8 million. We must admit that taxation can be so high that it creates a damaging effect on the ability of the people to buy, and when that happens the prosperity of a country begins to slip. I contend that the more money the people have the more they will buy, and the more they buy the more revenues will be collected. I think the government would be well-advised not to tax the people beyond their ability to buy.
I should like to make a few remarks in regard to the income tax. We know that the income tax is here to stay. It is one medium the government has in order to collect revenue, and we accept it; but I do think all medical and hospital expenses should be deductible. It is not reasonable that a taxpayer with a medical bill up to a certain percentage of his net income, and which is absolutely unavoidable, should not be able to deduct it as an expense.
We hear all kinds of complaints, especially from the small towns and rural districts, regarding the tax inspectors chasing the people for years back before they can obtain a clear receipt for taxes paid.
I contend that this should not be. Surely the staff is large enough now to process the tax returns within a reasonable length of time and give the taxpayer a clear receipt except in the case of fraud. The people are getting sick and tired of having a couple of inspectors calling on them long after they have either lost their receipts or forgotten the information they are asked for. If only one inspector called perhaps they would not mind it so much, but when the department

The Budget-Division came into Canada, much below the price of Canadian cheddar cheese, did the consumer receive the benefit of a lower price tag on the cheese they bought at the grocery? No.
I should like at this time to give figures concerning one of the milk plants in my constituency. We have three milk plants in the county of Leeds, together with many cheese factories, and I should like to give these figures to show the members of this house, and I hope the people of Canada, the decreased revenue of the farmers. In this one plant in 1951 the average price of milk was $3.15 per hundredweight; in 1952 it was $2.75; in 1953 it was $2.33.
